# CareStream content: house style and rules (applies to every page)

Read this first. Then read the page type guideline (collection, blog, or audit page) and the research file.

## Who we write for
A registered manager, owner, nominated individual, deputy or training lead at a small to medium CQC registered service in England: residential care homes, nursing homes, domiciliary care, supported living. No compliance department. Short of time. Knows their service well and the regulations reasonably well. Wants plain answers, evidence they can show an inspector, and no sales pressure. Respect their expertise. Never patronise.

## Tone
British, calm, plain, professional, specific. Let specifics persuade. Never use fear, countdowns or pressure. The fear is already in the room.

## Language rules (checked by a script, so follow exactly)
- British English only (organise, programme, licence as a noun, centre).
- We or CareStream. Never I.
- No em dashes or en dashes anywhere. Use a comma, full stop or colon. Hyphens only where the word truly takes one.
- No bold or italics in body text. Only headings are emphasised. No markdown tables of competitor text longer than needed (a comparison table is allowed in comparison posts).
- Banned words and phrases: crafted, solution(s), leverage, utilise, seamless, effortless, cutting edge, revolutionary, game changing, instant, instantly, immediate, immediately, guarantee (about ratings, inspections or approval), CQC compliant, CQC approved, cheap, cheapest, lowest price, bargain, clearance, limited time, limited stock, act now, hurry, flash sale, "in today's fast paced world", "it is important to note", "delve", "navigate the complexities", "ever evolving", "unlock".
- Say care settings or services. Only say care homes when residential or nursing homes are meant.
- Say residents or the people a service supports, as fits the setting.
- Name a regulation in full at least once before its short form. Spell out an acronym on first use.
- Full regulatory names, used at least once on any page that discusses regulation: the Care Quality Commission, the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, the Single Assessment Framework.
- Never say or imply that holding a policy, completing a course or running an audit guarantees a rating or inspection outcome.
- No calendar dates or years in content (see section 6 of 25-blog-formats-and-images.md). Freshness goes in `last_reviewed` and `review_by` front matter.
- Show CareStream prices as tokens such as {{price:policy_single_from}} (values in product-facts.json). Never "contact us for pricing". Never state competitor prices.
- Never lead with AI as the reason to use CareStream. Say what is produced, who uses it and what it records.

## Honesty rules (the most important)
- Never invent features, prices, statistics, reviews, quotes, awards, customer names or regulations. Only state facts you have verified from (a) the CareStream code or live site, (b) an authoritative source you fetched (CQC, GOV.UK, Skills for Care, NHS England, legislation.gov.uk, HSE, Food Standards Agency), or (c) the competitor's own page.
- NO [CHECK] MARKERS. Pages are auto-published, so nothing unverified may remain. Every factual claim (regulation, number, date, legal duty, competitor fact, statistic) is either (a) confirmed against a primary source you actually fetched, with its URL in `sources` and the date in `facts_verified`, (b) reworded as plainly our own recommendation ("we suggest", "in our view"), or (c) cut. If you cannot verify it, cut it. `unverified` must be empty. Keep a short claims log in the file after the body (claim, source URL, quote of 10 words or fewer).
- Competitor facts (price, features, limits): state only what their own page says, say where it came from, and add "at the time of writing" with the date. Be fair. Name what they do well. Never disparage.
- Never copy competitor text. Do not paraphrase closely. Write from our own knowledge and our product.
- Regulation facts must be correct and current. If unsure, fetch the primary source; if it cannot be confirmed, cut the claim.
- The CPD Certified mark and the words "CPD certified" apply only to the 10 certified courses.
- CareStream does not award the Care Certificate. The employer signs it off after observing practical skills. Say so wherever it matters.

## What CareStream actually offers (verified facts for this pilot)
Free plan (no card needed, free for ever, upgrade any time and keep everything):
- CPD certified training free for every member of staff: the Care Certificate and nine annual courses (COSHH, End of Life / Palliative Care, Food Hygiene, GDPR / Data Protection, General Health & Safety Awareness, Infection Prevention and Control, Medication Administration and Competency, Mental Health Awareness, Moving and Handling of People). Certificates are included. Access does not expire. In English on the free plan; 60+ languages start on the Starter plan.
- A training matrix for the CPD courses.
- Every audit template (30 audits) with reports, signatures and action tracking. AI recommendations at the end of an audit are on paid plans.
- Gap analysis on the first 5 policies (regulation coverage, out of date content, consistency, wording aligned to the CQC quality statements). More policies and example wording for every gap are on paid plans.
- As many staff logins as needed.
Paid plans: Starter £85 a month, Professional £230, Enterprise £385, each with a 14 day free trial (card required) . Written policies can also be bought from the policy shop (single policy £39 to £79, themed pack from £295, twenty statutory documents £495, written for the service, hand checked, delivered within two working days).
Always check the live site (carestreamai.com) and the repository (~/Care_Stream-wt-freecpd2) before relying on any detail.

## Links
- Internal links: choose from https://www.carestreamai.com/sitemap.xml. Only link to URLs that exist. Descriptive, long tail anchor text that describes the destination. Never "click here". Never bold or italicise anchors.
- Frame internal links as relationships: which pages belong together, which product a guide supports, how a single page relates to the wider CareStream platform.
- External links: only authoritative sources (CQC, GOV.UK, legislation.gov.uk, Skills for Care, NHS England, Skills for Health, HSE, Food Standards Agency, NICE). Put them in front matter `sources` as {label, url} and link naturally in the text. Competitor links appear only in comparison pages, plainly labelled.

## Images
Every page needs images with alt text. Rules and the image library are in 25-blog-formats-and-images.md.

## Output format
One Markdown file per page in ~/carestream-content/pilot/<family>/<slug>.md with front matter like this:

---
type: collection | blog | audit-page
family: care-certificate | audits | policies
title: ...
slug: ... (collections begin /collection/, blogs /blog/, audit pages /audits/ or the path given in the brief)
primary_keyword: ...
secondary_keywords: [..]
meta_title: ... (under 70 characters, ends | CareStream)
meta_description: ... (140 to 155 characters)
category: advice | guides (blogs only)
excerpt: ... (one or two sentences)
internal_links: [full URLs used]
sources: [{label: ..., url: ...}]
faqs: [{q: ..., a: ...}]
last_reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD
review_by: YYYY-MM-DD
format: A to H (the format letter from the brief, see 25-blog-formats-and-images.md)
feature_image: https://... (a real image URL)
feature_image_alt: ...
images: [{url: ..., alt: ..., role: feature|inline|grid}]
unverified: [list of every [CHECK] item]
---

Then the body in Markdown: H1 as `# `, then headings `##` and `###`. Plain paragraphs and lists. No bold or italics. Write FAQs in the front matter (and the page renders them), not in the body.


## Paragraph, sentence and link discipline (enforced by tools/lint.py, hard limits)
- Paragraph: 70 words maximum, aim 40 to 55. At most 3 sentences (4 only if under 60 words). One idea per paragraph. Start with the point, not the setup.
- Sentence: 28 words maximum. At most ONE legal reference per sentence (a Regulation, an Act, a Code of practice, statutory guidance). Several references become a short list. Gloss each in plain English on first use, for example "Regulation 13 (the duty to protect people from abuse)". Say who must do what: "the manager must tell the Care Quality Commission", not "the duty to notify".
- Reading: page grade 9 or lower; no paragraph above grade 11. Examples and disclaimers get their own short paragraph. Use a list or table where a section lists rules or steps; a subheading at least every 150 words.
- External links: only primary sources (legislation.gov.uk, gov.uk, cqc.org.uk, Skills for Care, NHS England, HSE, FSA, ICO, SCIE). Anchor text names what the reader gets in 3 or more words, for example "the full text of Regulation 12 on safe care and treatment". Never a bare domain ("legislation.gov.uk"), never "here", "source" or "link". One external link per paragraph, never in a heading, placed on the claim it supports, not as a trailing "Read it on ...". Do not paste a quotation and then link the domain: link the words that name the document. External links open in a new tab with rel noopener (the converter adds this).

# Collection page guideline (adapted from Len's collection template)

You write long form, search optimised collection page copy for CareStream. A collection page groups a family of products (a course, a set of audits, a set of policy checks) and explains them completely, so that a manager or an AI assistant could rely on the page alone.

## Structure (follow exactly)
1. H1 containing the target keyword.
2. Introduction, 150 to 200 words, before the first H2:
   - target keyword exactly twice in the introduction
   - first use within the first 25 words, second use within the first 50 words
   - active voice; purpose and benefits of the collection
3. The exact line on its own: {product-grid}
4. Body:
   - begins with an H2 (never another H1); at least two H2s; the first H2 is benefit led
   - at least four H3s, each section at least 100 words
   - one H3 explaining who this is perfect for
   - one H3 explaining why CareStream is better than the usual alternatives (be fair and accurate, no disparagement; refer to the kinds of alternatives, name competitors only if the brief says so)
   - expand on what is included, how it works, what it records, who it suits
   - at least one commercial word in an H2 or H3 heading from: free, get started, sign up, no card needed, no contract, upgrade any time, compare, value, available, included
   - no bold or italics outside headings
5. Slug beginning /collection/
6. 10 meta titles (each under 70 characters, each containing one different strong word, each ending | CareStream). Choose the best as meta_title in front matter and list all 10 at the end of the file under "Meta title options".
7. One meta description, 140 to 155 characters.
8. 15 FAQs written from the People Also Ask and related searches in the research file, in natural English, with plain accurate answers. They must reinforce who needs this, what triggers it, what is included, how long it takes, what it costs (free, and what paid plans add) and what happens if they upgrade or stop.

## Keyword rules
- Target keyword: 3 to 4 times in total on the page (the introduction twice counts).
- Brand name CareStream: exactly three times in the whole page body.
- Each secondary keyword: exactly once, placed naturally.
- Write for people first. Never stuff keywords.

## Links and headings in the copy below the product grid (hard rules, 18 Nov 2026)
The copy below the grid is where a collection earns its authority, so it must carry real links and a clean outline. The checker enforces all of this.
- Internal links: at least three different internal links in the copy below {product-grid}, every URL taken from the live sitemap (never invented). Anchors are long tail and descriptive (for example "free moving and handling course for care staff", "the training matrix that tracks renewals"), never "here", "click here", "read more", or a bare page name used for every link. Link to the most relevant free course, audit, policy page, feature page, related collection or blog post for what the paragraph says, and spread them through different sections, not all in one paragraph.
- External links: at least two different external links to PRIMARY sources (legislation.gov.uk, gov.uk, cqc.org.uk, nice.org.uk, hse.gov.uk, skillsforcare.org.uk, nhs.uk, ico.org.uk and similar), each placed on the exact claim it supports (the regulation, the code of practice, the guidance), with an anchor that names the document (3 or more words, for example "full text of Regulation 12 on safe care and treatment"), never a domain name or "source". Fetch every external URL first and confirm it returns 200 and says what you claim. Maximum one external link per paragraph, never in a heading.
- Headings: everything below the grid is organised with real H2 and H3 headings only. The first heading is an H2, there are at least two H2s and at least four H3s, no level is skipped, no H1 or H4 or lower is used, and no bold line, label ending in a colon or capitalised line stands in for a heading. Each H2 or H3 says what the section answers (a question or a clear statement), and the H3s sit under the H2 they belong to.
- The links must be visible to the reader: they render in the accent colour with an underline. Do not wrap link text in bold.

## Internal links
Two or three internal links in the body from the sitemap, with long tail descriptive anchors. (Superseded by the rules above: at least three internal and two external.)

## LLM discoverability (write the page as a complete explanation)
- Explain what this collection is, who must or should use it, why, and when people look for it.
- Connect each item to the regulation it addresses, the care setting it applies to and the situation that prompts it.
- Define terms in full on first use, for example infection prevention and control, not IPC.
- Use explanatory paragraphs for "who has to hold or do this", naming residential care homes, nursing homes, domiciliary care agencies, supported living and hospices where relevant.
- Use the questions people actually ask as the basis for headings and FAQs.
- Be correct above all. An AI model may repeat this page.

## Persona for the three families
- Care Certificate / CPD training: a registered manager, owner or training lead who must induct new starters, evidence mandatory training to the Care Quality Commission, and cannot afford per learner fees or a spreadsheet of expiry dates.
- Audits: a registered manager or deputy who runs monthly audits on paper or in spreadsheets, has to show governance, and has seen audit software gated behind trials and per user pricing.
- Policies: a registered manager, owner or nominated individual of a small service with no compliance department, who needs to know what they hold, what is missing and what is out of date.


## Page intent and commercial keywords (added 14 November 2026)
Collections are the high commercial intent pages: this is where people buy, or sign up for the free product. Blog posts are informational. They are different jobs and carry different keywords.
- A collection carries a SMALL, natural selection of commercial words (3 to 8 distinct, from guidelines/commercial-terms.json), at least one in an H2 or H3, matched to what the page really offers:
  * Free CPD courses, free audits and the free policy check still have commercial intent: free, get started, sign up, try, available, compare, upgrade (to paid plan features).
  * Paid policies: price (always a token), buy, order, purchase, bundle, basket, checkout, shop, delivery, refund, with only the facts verified in the code or on the live product page.
  * Paid plan features: pricing, plans, upgrade, free trial, subscription, pay monthly, book a demo, choose plan, compare plans.
- Only true words. No cheap, discount, deals, limited time, free shipping, warranty, in stock, clearance, best value and the other words listed as forbidden: they are either untrue for CareStream or unverifiable, and the house rules ban superlatives. A word like "no contract", "cancel anytime" or "secure checkout" is used only after it is verified.
- Natural beats many. One commercial word in a heading and two or three in the copy is enough; never a list of them.


## Paid policy pages (added 16 Nov 2026)
The shop now sells 148 paid policies: the original 66 plus 82 added in three waves (22 care homes, home care and supported living; 26 more adult social care; 34 for children's homes and for hospices and specialist services). The full list, with each page's URL, price, services, primary keyword and secondary keywords, is in ledger/policy-catalogue.json (readable version: ledger/policy-catalogue.md). When you write a collection:
- link to the relevant policy page (/care-policies/<slug>) where it genuinely helps the reader, and prefer the policies for the service the page is about;
- never target a policy page's primary keyword: that page owns it. Use its secondary keywords only as supporting phrases;
- take prices from the product-facts tokens, never from the catalogue file.

Policy packs (added 16 Nov 2026): ledger/policy-packs.json lists the seven new pack pages (/care-policies/packs/<key>) with their keywords. A collection about a service may link to the matching pack. Never target a pack page's primary keyword.

# NOTE: read 25-blog-formats-and-images.md FIRST. Where it conflicts with this file (single common skeleton, hook intro, Short answer, Where CareStream fits, Conclusion), 25 wins. Keep this file's rules on length, links, sources, FAQs, comparison fairness, tone and the audit page content.

# Blog post guideline (adapted from Len's blog template)

Target 1,300 to 1,800 words unless the brief says otherwise. Helpful, objective, skimmable, peer to peer. No marketing fluff. No bold or italic text anywhere. British English. Do not use hyphens to replace commas.

## Common structure for guides
1. H1 with the primary keyword.
2. Hook introduction (80 to 130 words): start with the situation the reader is in, say plainly what the post answers. Primary keyword in the first 25 words.
3. "Short answer" block (two to four sentences or a short list) that directly answers the main question, for readers and for AI answers.
4. Body with H2s and H3s that contain the keywords and related questions naturally (taken from People Also Ask). Each H2 answers one question fully.
5. A practical element: a checklist, a schedule, a step by step, or a worked example.
6. Regulation grounding where relevant: name the Care Quality Commission, the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 and the specific regulation, and the Single Assessment Framework where it applies. Link to the primary source.
7. "Where CareStream fits" (one short H2): how the free product helps, factual, no hard sell. CareStream mentioned three to five times in the post.
8. Conclusion paragraph (required) that tells the reader what to do next.
9. FAQs in the front matter (5 to 8, from People Also Ask).
10. Commercial words, used naturally and sparingly (not all): free, get started, sign up, no card needed, no contract, upgrade any time, compare, value, available, included.

## Comparison posts (the "alternatives" format)
Used only when the brief says so. Follow the Zapier style:
1. Hook intro with a relatable problem; say we researched and compared the options and when we did it.
2. "At a glance" bulleted list of winners by use case.
3. Methodology H2: "What makes the best [thing]?" with three clear criteria.
4. Comparison table (Markdown): Brand, Best for, Standout feature, Starting price. CareStream is always listed first. Use only verified prices and quote the date checked. Write "not stated on their site" when a price is not published.
5. A deep dive H2 for each option: "Best for [use case] | [Brand]" with pros and cons (bulleted), a two or three paragraph review about who should choose it, and a "Starting at" line stating the verified price with the date.
6. Conclusion on how to choose, and a clear call to action to try CareStream free.
Fairness: acknowledge what competitors do well (for example NHS England eLfH offers free Care Certificate e-learning). Never claim CareStream is the only free option unless verified.

## Audit page guideline (audit detail pages)
A page for one specific audit that we offer free. Structure:
1. H1: "[Audit name] audit template for care services" (or as the brief says).
2. Short answer: what the audit is, who runs it, how often, what it evidences.
3. What this audit covers: group the real question set into sections (read it from the CareStream audit seed in the repository; do not invent questions). Show the actual questions as lists, grouped by section.
4. Who should run it and how often (reasoned, cite sources, mark [CHECK] where frequency is our recommendation rather than a rule).
5. Which regulation and CQC quality statements it helps evidence (verify; do not overclaim).
6. How to score it and turn findings into an action plan (link to what CareStream does: scoring, signatures, action tracking, reports are free; AI recommendations are on paid plans).
7. Run this audit free (call to action), FAQs in front matter.


## Paid policy pages (added 16 Nov 2026)
The shop now sells 148 paid policies: the original 66 plus 82 added in three waves (22 care homes, home care and supported living; 26 more adult social care; 34 for children's homes and for hospices and specialist services). The full list, with each page's URL, price, services, primary keyword and secondary keywords, is in ledger/policy-catalogue.json (readable version: ledger/policy-catalogue.md). When you write a blog post:
- link to the relevant policy page (/care-policies/<slug>) where it genuinely helps the reader, and prefer the policies for the service the page is about;
- never target a policy page's primary keyword: that page owns it. Use its secondary keywords only as supporting phrases;
- take prices from the product-facts tokens, never from the catalogue file.

## Pace (changed 16 Nov 2026)
Blog creation goes up from 3 to 4 posts a night, from the evening of 16 Nov 2026. Len's reason: the content is good. The ramp rule in 40-learning-system.md still applies (raise further only while pages are being indexed and the quality sample holds). Every post still goes through the checker and a human review sample; nothing publishes without passing it.

Policy packs (added 16 Nov 2026): seven new packs have their own pages. See ledger/policy-packs.json for the packs, the policies in each and each pack page's primary and secondary keywords. Link to a pack from posts about that service (for example the children's homes pack from a children's home post), and never target a pack page's primary keyword.

# Blog formats, openings and images (this OVERRIDES the single skeleton in 20-blog-guideline.md)

Problem we are fixing: our first drafts all opened the same way ("If you have searched...", "Sooner or later every manager asks...", then "This guide explains...") and then ran the same sections in the same order (Short answer, Who must..., What the law says, Where CareStream fits, Conclusion). Readers and search engines notice. Every page must now be built on its own FORMAT, with its own opening move and its own shape.

## 1. Assign one format per page (the brief tells you which)
A. WALKTHROUGH: follow one real task in order, in time order or step order. Opens inside the task (the first action), not with a summary.
B. WORKED EXAMPLE: start from a short, clearly labelled illustrative scenario ("Here is an example, not a real case") and show how the policy, audit or training answers it, step by step.
C. INSPECTOR'S QUESTIONS: build the page around the questions an inspector or auditor actually asks, each answered with what evidence to show. Opens with the most awkward question.
D. MYTH BUSTER: open with the common wrong belief, state it in one line, then correct it with evidence. Each section tackles one belief.
E. CALENDAR OR SCHEDULE: lead with the schedule itself (a table or list) in the first screen, then explain the reasoning and how to adapt it.
F. DECISION GUIDE (comparison): open with the decision the reader faces and the cost of getting it wrong; then criteria, then options.
G. REFERENCE EXPLAINER: a clean reference to look things up in (a list of defined items), opened with the single fact most readers get wrong.
H. TEMPLATE PAGE (audit pages): the template is the content. Opens with what the audit is for in one sentence.

## 2. Opening rules (checked by script)
- The first paragraph must be concrete: a situation, a fact, a number, a mistake, a question an inspector asks. It must NOT summarise the article.
- Banned openers and phrases anywhere in the first 150 words: "this guide", "in this guide", "this article", "this post", "this page explains", "if you have searched", "if you are looking for", "if you are", "sooner or later", "whether you", "the honest answer", "in this article", "we will cover", "let us look", "you need to".
- Do not put the primary keyword in the first sentence unless it reads naturally. It must appear within the first 120 words and in the H1.
- Vary sentence openings across the page. No page may start with the same first six words as any other page.

## 3. Structure rules
- Use only the sections the format needs. A "Short answer" block is OPTIONAL; if used, vary its heading ("The short version", "Quick answer", or none) and its position.
- No fixed "Who must hold this", "What the law says", "Where CareStream fits" scaffold. Include regulation grounding and the CareStream mention where they genuinely help, in a place and wording that suits the format. Do not reuse the same H2 text as another page.
- No heading may be shared by more than one page (the script checks). Mix heading styles: some questions, some statements, some with numbers.
- Do not end with a heading called Conclusion. End the way the format ends (the last step, the final checklist, the decision, the next action).
- Length follows the format: 900 to 2,000 words. Do not pad.
- Avoid repeating signature phrases: "our recommendation, not a rule", "the honest answer", "in practice". Say it differently each time or leave it out.

## 4. Real material only we have (information gain)
Each page must contain at least two things a competitor's page would not: for example the real question set of a CareStream audit, how the course is built (length, number of questions, what the certificate shows), the 16 standards mapped, what the gap check actually looks for, what the free account records. Use product facts from the repository and the live site. If an observation needs a person's real experience, leave a line "[LEN: add a real observation about X]" and list it under `unverified`.

## 5. IMAGES (every page)
Real CareStream product images already exist. Choose from these and OPEN EACH ONE (use the Read tool, it can view images) before using it, so the alt text describes what it really shows.
- Training and matrix: /Users/lenburgess/Care_Stream-wt-freecpd2/apps/web/public/cpd-course-summary.jpg, cpd-module-complete.jpg, cpd-observation-checklist.jpg, cpd-training-hub.jpg, matrix-training-calendar.jpg, matrix-f2f-matrix.jpg, reporting-training-matrix.jpg, reporting-staff-record.jpg, reporting-completion-email.jpg, why-carestream-training.jpg, follow-up-hub.jpg
- Course illustrations (live, one per CPD course): https://api.carestreamai.com/public/training/image/<id>.webp. Care Certificate: 54e69828-2107-4f9c-b159-91dadc35ec6e; Moving and handling: b3cb23d1-b634-47ca-848d-fef4df7eb4c0; Infection prevention and control: d291f197-9e24-4a6b-be0a-fa78b2560e9b; Medication: e296053a-d3f1-4904-938a-209dcf448755; Food hygiene: 4e927af4-e903-4170-8794-ac4e0d4bbf32; GDPR: 26164b66-ef1e-469a-a142-cdcb90429190; General health and safety: c47a84d5-032c-46e6-8a19-686a752d4d96; COSHH: 7766c9c5-8aa1-469e-817f-8b7eba7d3117; Mental health: 9fafd949-a86e-4736-adf2-ef87908824da; End of life: efb1bf12-df62-4ead-8efa-2c8f13af5aa7. (Download to view if needed.)
- Audits: .../public/emails/audit-library.jpg, audit-report.jpg, audit-action-plan.jpg, audit-signatures.jpg, audit-scheduling.jpg, audit-trends.jpg, audit-photo-evidence.jpg, audit-builder.jpg, audit-import.jpg; also .../public/email-previews/audits-hub.jpg and audits.png
- Policies and gap check: .../public/platform-policy-preview.jpg, email-previews/policy-gap-detection.png, gaps.png, mock-policy-library.jpg, mock-policy-out-of-date.jpg, mock-policy-adopted.jpg, mock-team-gaps.jpg, mock-policies-missing.jpg; regulation images in .../public/images/policy-law/*.webp (for example health-and-social-care-act-infection-control-code.webp); .../public/images/care-policies/1.webp to 4.webp
- New library (16 Nov 2026): library/images.json lists the hero image for every policy added in waves 1 to 3 (82) and every regulation image (policy-law), with live URLs. Pick from it by topic, open the image before use, and record the page in the image's `used_on`. The original 66 policy heroes are at .../public/images/care-policies/<slug>/1.webp (one per policy page).
- Live URL for any public file: https://www.carestreamai.com/<path under public>.
Rules:
- Every page: one FEATURE image (front matter `feature_image` and `feature_image_alt`) plus, for blogs, 1 to 3 inline images; collections one feature image plus at most 1 inline image in the main content (the product grid carries the rest); audit pages 2 to 3. Place inline images where they support the text, with a short plain caption line under each (a normal paragraph starting with "Figure:" is fine, no italics).
- Inline syntax: ![alt text](https://www.carestreamai.com/path.jpg)
- ALT TEXT: describe what the image actually shows and why it matters to the reader, 70 to 125 characters, plain sentence, no "image of", "picture of" or "screenshot of" at the start, no keyword stuffing (use a keyword only if it truly describes the image), no dashes, British English, specific (name the screen and what is visible, for example "CareStream audit report showing section scores and the failed items listed with actions").
- Staff incentives screens (live): https://www.carestreamai.com/images/features/staff-incentives/1.webp to 5.webp (admin builder, hub points tracker, approvals, results).
- BLOG HERO RULE (hard, checked by script): the feature image (hero) of every blog is ALWAYS generated fresh for that post, with POST /routine/content/image (house style: flat teal illustration, people with simple friendly faces and open visible eyes, no text, no screens). Never use a stock, library, course, policy or regulation illustration as a blog hero, even if one seems to fit. Write a scene that shows the post's own situation (who is doing what, where), not a generic care image. Do NOT describe anyone's ethnicity, skin tone or age in the scene: the image endpoint assigns a different, varied cast to each picture (and a different person in each position) from the key you send, so use a unique key per image, such as hero-<slug>. Generate the hero first, look at the result, and regenerate once if it has closed eyes, text, a screen or the wrong scene. The order of choice below applies to INLINE images and to collections.
- ORDER OF CHOICE for every inline image slot (and for a collection's one feature image) (blogs: feature plus inline; collections: ONE feature image in the main content is enough, do not generate extra inline art for a collection):
  1. A real product screenshot or mock-up from the lists above when the page is about a CareStream feature, screen or workflow. Open it first and describe what it really shows. Mock-ups and real screenshots are welcome inside blog posts: use one wherever it makes the point concrete (for example the audit report, the training matrix, the This is me profile, the incentives tracker).
  2. NEVER a stock, course, policy-hero or regulation illustration (anything under /public/training/image/, /images/policy-law/ or /images/care-policies/<slug>/, or listed as policy-hero or regulation in library/images.json). They are the old image style and are banned as inline images in blogs and collections, exactly as they are banned as heroes. The lint fails the page. Only real product screenshots and mock-ups (option 1) are allowed besides a freshly generated image.
  3. For every other inline slot, GENERATE one in the house style (flat teal, people with simple friendly faces and open visible eyes, no text, no screens). Do this with the image endpoint, never with any other service: POST https://api.carestreamai.com/routine/content/image with the same Authorization header, JSON {"topic": "<page topic>", "scene": "<one or two sentences describing ONE ordinary believable care moment that shows the point in practice>", "key": "<page slug>"}. It returns {"url": ...}. curl the url to confirm HTTP 200 and an image type, open it with the Read tool to check it (no lettering, nothing distressing, nothing odd with hands or faces) and write the alt text from what you actually see. If it looks wrong, ask once more with a clearer scene; if it is still wrong, fall back to `[CHECK] new image needed`. The endpoint allows 24 images a day in total: one hero per blog, at most 2 generated inline images per blog and 1 per collection, which fits four blogs and six collections a night (4 x 3 + 6 = 18 of 24). Never skip generation to save the budget: if the limit is reached, flag [CHECK] new image needed instead of using a stock illustration. A generated image counts as unique to that page.
  4. A real screenshot of a CareStream screen that does not exist yet cannot be taken by the routine. Add `[CHECK] screenshot needed: <which screen, what state>` to `unverified` and use a generated or stock image meanwhile; Len has the screenshot taken from the live platform.
- ACCURACY OF PRODUCT IMAGES (a hard rule, the most important image rule). A screenshot or mock-up must show only what the CareStream platform really does today. Never invent a screen, button, report, score, menu item, plan feature or workflow. Specifically:
  * Use only the real screenshots and mock-ups listed in this guideline or in library/images.json. Open each one and describe only what is visibly there.
  * Check the picture against ledger/audit-features.md, product-facts.json, guidelines and the feature pages. If the text of the post mentions a capability the image shows, that capability must be confirmed in those files; if you cannot confirm it, do not use the image for that claim.
  * Never generate a picture of the CareStream app, a dashboard, a software screen, a report layout or any interface with the image endpoint. The endpoint makes scene illustrations of people and places only. Generated images must never contain screens with readable or implied interface content, charts with labels, logos or invented product UI.
  * Never edit, redraw or compose a new mock-up. A new mock-up or screenshot is made only from the live platform by Len's team. If you need one, add `[CHECK] screenshot needed: <screen and state>` to `unverified`.
  * If an image may show an older interface, add `[CHECK] image may be out of date` and prefer a newer one.
  * The alt text and the surrounding sentence must describe the screen exactly as it is, not what it could become. Plan gates matter: if a feature is on Professional or Enterprise only, say so when you show it (check product-facts.json).
- THE FEATURE IMAGE IS NEVER REPEATED IN THE BODY. The `feature_image` is the hero at the top of the page, so the same file must not appear as an inline image (especially not as the first image under the opening paragraph). Every inline image is a different file from the feature image. Check this before saving; the lint fails the page if it happens. If you only have one suitable image, generate a second one (order of choice, step 3) rather than repeating it or using a library image.
- Never use an image whose content contradicts the text. A screenshot shows the product as it is today; never imply a feature the product does not have.
- Only choose images whose content fits the point. If no existing image fits and generation is not possible (limit reached or the result is unusable), do not force one: add `[CHECK] new image needed: <description>` to `unverified`.
- If a product screenshot may show an older interface than the live product, note `[CHECK] image may be out of date`.
- List all images in front matter as `images:` with {url, alt, role: feature|inline|grid} for the CMS.

## 6. EVERGREEN RULES (added 13 November 2026, checked by script)
Pages must stay true for years. So:
- NO calendar dates or years in the body, title, meta title, meta description, slug, FAQs or alt text. No "13 November", no "in 2026", no "March 2025", no "by 1 March".
  Allowed: the names of laws and codes that contain a year (Care Act 2014, Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, Equality Act 2010). Also the phrase "the 2025 update" at most twice per page where it names a real, searchable event.
- NO time-relative words: currently, recently, latest, this year, next year, last year, at the time of writing, as of, nowadays, newly. Say what is true without a time anchor. For deadlines, use relative rules ("within twelve weeks of the start date").
- Examples and scenarios must not use dates ("On a Monday...", "At twenty to eight...").
- Freshness lives in front matter, not prose: add `last_reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD` and `review_by: YYYY-MM-DD` (three months ahead for comparison pages, twelve months for others).
- NO raw prices. Any CareStream price or changeable number is a token from guidelines/product-facts.json, written like {{price:policy_single_from}} or {{count:audits}}. If a token you need is missing, add it to product-facts.json with the verified value and list it in your report.
- NO competitor prices or terms that change. Describe how a competitor charges (free, per learner, subscription, one off bundle) and say "check their site for the current price". Do not state their price, discount or limits.
- Comparison pages are "maintained", not evergreen: they carry `review_by` three months ahead and the nightly system re-checks them. Their prose still has no dates.

## 7. DISTINCTIVENESS (added after the first two Care Certificate posts still read alike)
Pages in the same topic cluster must feel written for different questions by a thinking person, not generated from one template.
- ONE IDEA PER PAGE. Each page owns one question. Do not re-explain what a sibling page owns: link to it with one line. Two pages must not share a hook (for example "most providers still say 15 standards").
- OPEN ON SOMETHING ONLY THIS PAGE CAN SAY: a specific, surprising detail, a number from our own product, a precise mistake. Not a general framing of the topic.
- VOICE. Each brief assigns a voice. Reviewer voice: opinionated, first person plural, "we would pick", trade offs stated. Teacher voice: second person, explains, defines, walks the reader through. Practitioner voice: situation led, short scene, then the lesson. Inspector voice: question and evidence. Use the assigned voice throughout.
- RHYTHM. Vary sentence length deliberately: a mix of very short sentences (3 to 7 words), medium (12 to 20) and a few long ones (24 to 30). Average still about 15 to 17. Never ten sentences in a row of similar length. The checker measures the spread.
- NO SHARED BOILERPLATE. Do not write "we checked these sources", "we flag what we could not confirm", "prices and offers change, so confirm", "here is an example, not a real case" in the same words on more than one page. Provenance and review notes are handled by the site (`last_reviewed`, a standard "how we review" note), not repeated in prose. A labelled scenario says it is an example once, in its own words.
- NO SHARED SENTENCES. No sentence may appear (or nearly appear) on more than one page. If two pages need the same fact, state it differently or link instead.
- IMAGES. A feature image is used on one page only. An inline image appears on at most two pages in total, and two posts in the same family do not share an image. Choose images that fit the page's own point; if no image fits, add `[CHECK] new image needed`.


INLINE IMAGE STYLE RULE (added 20 Nov 2026): every illustration anywhere in the main content of a blog or collection is generated fresh with the same endpoint and house style as the hero. Scenes must avoid bedrooms, beds, personal care, hoists and anyone undressed (the image service blocks them): use lounges, corridors, offices, kitchens, gardens and doorways instead. Write the alt text from what the generated image actually shows.

# How the content engine learns (design)

Goal: every page we publish teaches the system something, and the rules, the opening library, the formats and the topic priorities change as the evidence arrives. Humans approve rule changes. The system never raises its own limits.

## 1. Tag every page with its "genes" (the ledger)
For each page the ledger (ledger/content-ledger.json, later a database table) records what we chose, so we can later ask which choices worked:
- topic family, product, search intent, primary keyword, keyword volume and difficulty at the time
- format (A to H), voice, opening type (library/openings.json), ending type, title pattern, meta description pattern
- length band, number and type of images, number of internal links, schema types, call to action type and position
- dates: created, published, indexed, last reviewed, review by
- human edits made at review (category: tone, claim, structure, facts, links)
tools/ledger.py already registers the first set from each page's front matter.

## 2. Measure, with the right metric for each gene
Data: Google Search Console (page and query level) and GA4 (landing page behaviour and key events), joined to the ledger by URL. Both are already connected (traffic reports service account).
| What we changed | Best signal | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Title, meta description | Click through rate at comparable position | Only thing the searcher sees before the click |
| Opening, voice, format, images | GA4 engaged sessions, engagement time, scroll depth, next click | These change what happens after the click, not rankings directly |
| Length, structure, headings, internal links | Impressions, average position, queries won, indexing | Affect how Google understands and ranks the page |
| Call to action | Free account sign ups (and clicks to register) by landing page | The goal of the product funnel |
| Topic family | Impressions and clicks growth over weeks | Shows whether a cluster is gaining authority |
Checkpoints per page: day 14 (indexed?), day 28 (impressions and queries?), day 56 to 84 (position, clicks, engagement, sign ups). Never judge a page earlier.

## 3. Be honest about the statistics
CareStream is a young site (about 22,000 impressions in 90 days across the whole domain), so a single page has little data. Therefore:
- Pool evidence across pages that share a gene (all pages with the "paper trail" opening), not one page at a time.
- Set minimum evidence before any conclusion (for example 500 impressions or 100 sessions per group). Below that the result is "not enough data", which is a valid outcome.
- Compare like with like (same family, similar keyword volume, similar age) and keep a control group of pages left unchanged.
- Report uncertainty. Do not attribute a site wide rise to one change.

## 4. Choose what to publish next: explore and exploit, but stay varied
- Each new page needs a format, voice, opening type and ending. The picker (tools/ledger.py next) chooses among eligible options using past performance, with a bandit approach: most picks favour what is working, but about a quarter explore under used or new options.
- Variety always beats performance. Recency rules (no opening type reused within 8 posts) and share caps (no move over 10 percent of posts once there are 20 or more) apply even to a winner. A site where every post opens the same way is a template, however well it scores.

## 5. Evolve the library
- Monthly learning review (automatic report, human decision): best and worst moves with evidence and uncertainty; proposed retirements; proposed new moves.
- New moves come from three places: variants the system proposes by combining or mutating winners; patterns in Search Console queries and People Also Ask (what readers literally ask); human edits at review.
- A new move starts at exploration weight. A move that stays below average with enough evidence is retired. The library is versioned (library/openings.json "version"); Len approves every change. So the twenty moves in use next quarter will not be the twenty today.
- The same mechanism applies to formats, voices, endings, title patterns and image types.

## 6. Learn from people
The strongest signal is what Len changes when reviewing. Each edit is logged by category (tone, claim, structure, facts, links, openings). Repeated edits of one kind become a proposed guideline change (for example "stop opening with niche details"), supported by the examples.

## 7. The lessons register
Every finding is recorded as: context, action, evidence, uncertainty, where it applies. A lesson becomes a rule only after repeated evidence or a verified mechanism. Rules are versioned with a changelog so we can see why a rule exists and undo it.

## 8. Opportunity discovery from the same data
- Search Console queries where we appear but rank poorly become the next briefs (query opportunities).
- Pages with impressions and low click through rate get a title or snippet test.
- Pages that lose position are refreshed at their review date.
- Competitor pages that start ranking for our keywords are re-researched.
- Later: whether AI assistants cite us for our topics (AI visibility).

## 9. Operating rhythm
- Daily: generate, run the quality gates, queue for review (later auto publish), record in the ledger.
- Weekly: pull Search Console and GA4 into the ledger; check day 14 and day 28 cohorts; send the learning report.
- Monthly: library and guideline review with evidence; Len approves changes.
- Quarterly: refresh pages whose review date is due; prune pages that failed after a fair trial.

## 10. Guardrails
- Ramp volume only when indexing and quality hold; stop automatically if indexing rate drops or the quality sample fails.
- A human reads a sample of every batch. Changes to rules, limits or authority need approval.
- Nothing is published that fails the checker. A page that fails twice goes back to the queue.
- Keep a rollback for every publish.

## 11. Build order
1. Ledger with genes (started: tools/ledger.py).
2. Daily pull of Search Console and GA4 by URL into the ledger (extend the existing traffic report scripts).
3. Weekly learning report by gene, with sample sizes and uncertainty.
4. Picker with exploration and variety constraints.
5. Monthly library proposals (new, mutated and retired moves) for approval.
6. Human edit logging.

# How one CareStream page is written and checked (blogs and collections)

This is the working process for the nightly job and for any agent asked to write a page. It does not replace the guidelines; it says in what order to use them. Read ALL of these first, in full, before writing a word:
1. guidelines/00-house-style.md
2. guidelines/25-blog-formats-and-images.md (OVERRIDES the skeleton in 20 for blogs: formats A to H, openings, evergreen rules, distinctiveness, images)
3. guidelines/20-blog-guideline.md (length, links, sources, FAQs, tone, policy page and pack rules)
4. guidelines/10-collection-guideline.md (collections only)
5. guidelines/commercial-terms.json and guidelines/product-facts.json (tokens for every price and changeable number)
6. research/serp-intel-uk-2026-11-13.md (what ranks, People Also Ask themes, who the competitors are)
7. ledger/policy-catalogue.json and ledger/policy-packs.json when the page touches policies; ledger/audit-features.md when it touches audits

## Steps
1. TOPIC. Take the brief you were given (backlog entry: primary keyword, volume, secondary keywords, format, voice, product, what to verify). Never target a keyword another page owns (lint warns; ledger/content-ledger.json lists every page's primary keyword; the platform list of existing slugs is in the brief).
2. OPENING. Run `python3 tools/ledger.py next <FORMAT>` and use the opening type assigned in your brief (or the top suggestion). Record it as `opening_type` in front matter.
3. RESEARCH AND VERIFY. Every factual claim about law, CQC, NICE, UKHSA, HSE or other bodies must be checked against the primary source (fetch the page). Keep a claims log at pilot/claims/<slug>.claims.md in the same shape as the existing ones (claim | short quote). A claim you cannot confirm is CUT, or kept only as a clearly labelled "[CHECK]" line listed under `unverified` in front matter. Do not invent statistics, dates, case examples or competitor facts. Never state a competitor price.
4. WRITE the page to the format and voice assigned. No bold or italics, no dashes used as commas, British English, no raw prices (tokens only), no calendar dates or years in prose (evergreen rules), no banned phrases. Include the information gain material (real CareStream product facts: the question set of a real audit, course length and question count, what the free account records). Choose images from the lists in guideline 25 and library/images.json, open each one with the Read tool before use, write alt text of 70 to 125 characters, respect the one feature image per page rule (check content-ledger.json and pilot/ for images already used).
5. FRONT MATTER exactly like the existing pages in pilot/ (see a sibling for the keys): type, last_reviewed, review_by, family, title, slug, topic_cluster, cta_type, primary_keyword, secondary_keywords, meta_title (under 70 characters, ends | CareStream), meta_description (140 to 155 characters), category, excerpt, internal_links (real URLs from the live sitemap https://www.carestreamai.com/sitemap.xml, never invented), sources (label + url), format, opening_type, voice, feature_image, feature_image_alt, images, faqs (blogs 5 to 8; collections 15), unverified, facts_verified.
6. SAVE the page at pilot/<family>/<slug>.md. Then run `python3 tools/render.py <file>` mentally: every {{token}} must exist in product-facts.json (add a verified token if needed and say so).
7. LINT. Run `python3 tools/lint.py pilot` (the whole folder, so the cross page sameness check sees every page). Your file must show PASS or WARN with no ERROR, and you must not cause an ERROR in another page. Fix and re-run until clean. Read each warning and fix what is real.
8. CONVERT (do not import): blogs `python3 tools/to_blogpost.py <out.json> <resolved file>`; collections `python3 tools/to_collection.py <out.json> <resolved file>` (both take the resolved copy from render.py, see how pilot-preview/ is produced).
9. REPORT: what you wrote, word count, the lint result, anything cut or unverified, tokens added, images used.

## Hard rules (a page that breaks any of these is rejected)
- Nothing is published. Pages are saved as drafts only; Len approves every one.
- Do not copy sentences from sibling pages; do not reuse a heading used by another page.
- Prices and counts come from tokens. Free product claims come from guidelines/product-facts.json and free-tier/facts.md (free: unlimited staff, all audits free, 5 lifetime policy check allowance, CPD courses free English only; paid: AI recommendations, translations, unlimited policies, adopting fixes).
- No superlatives, no disparagement, no claim that CareStream makes anyone "CQC compliant".

# Nightly routine prompts (the text each cloud routine runs)

Two routines: CareStream blogs (4 a night) and CareStream collections (6 a night: two training, two policy, two audit). Each saves DRAFTS only through the content routine API. Nothing publishes. Replace <TOKEN> with the CONTENT_ROUTINE_TOKEN value when creating the routine. Update this file and the routine together.

## Shared setup (both routines)

You are the nightly CareStream content writer for Len Burgess. You write pages that must follow the CareStream guidelines exactly. You save them as DRAFTS for human review; nothing you do publishes anything. There is no repository to clone. Everything goes through one HTTPS API. Use bash and python3.

API base: https://api.carestreamai.com/routine/content   Header on every request: `Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>`. Never print or echo the token. Set `AUTH="Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>"` once and use it.

1. Work in a folder: `mkdir -p ~/cs && cd ~/cs`.
2. Download the engine: `curl -s -H "$AUTH" https://api.carestreamai.com/routine/content/bundle -o bundle.json`, then with python3 write every entry of `data.files` to its relative path under `~/cs/` (the keys are paths such as `guidelines/00-house-style.md`, `tools/lint.py`). If the download fails, stop and report; do not write pages from memory.
3. Download the platform state: `curl -s -H "$AUTH" https://api.carestreamai.com/routine/content/state -o state_raw.json` and save `data` as `state.json`.
4. Create `pilot/` and `pilot/claims/` folders. Tools expect the files at `~/carestream-content`: run `ln -s ~/cs ~/carestream-content`.
5. Read, in full, before writing anything: guidelines/50-page-writing-process.md and every guideline it lists. These are the rules. When a rule and this prompt disagree, the guideline wins.
6. Pick tonight's topics: `python3 tools/pick_topics.py <blog|collection> <4 for blog, 6 for collection> state.json`. These are the topics; do not pick your own. If fewer than four come back, write what you have.

## For each topic (one at a time)
- Write the page exactly to guidelines/50-page-writing-process.md, with the format, voice and keywords in the topic entry. Open with an opening type from `python3 tools/ledger.py next <FORMAT>` that the recent pages have not used (a ledger is not kept across nights: also read the first paragraphs of the model pages in pilot/ and of the opening types listed in library/openings.json so you do not repeat a pattern; the platform state shows every existing page's first words in `first12`).
- Verify every factual claim by fetching the primary source (gov.uk, legislation.gov.uk, CQC, NICE, UKHSA, HSE, Skills for Care, NHS). Anything you cannot confirm is cut or listed under `unverified`. Never invent a statistic, a quote, a date, or a competitor fact.
- Product images must be accurate: only real screenshots and mock-ups from the library, never a picture of the app that you generate, and nothing that shows a feature the platform does not have (guideline 25, accuracy rule).
- Blog hero images: ALWAYS generate the feature image for each blog with POST /routine/content/image (never a stock, library, course or policy illustration; lint fails the post if the hero is not a generated image). Generate it before drafting the inline images, look at it, and regenerate once if it shows closed eyes, text, a screen or the wrong scene.
- Inline images and collections: follow the order of choice in guideline 25 section 5: real screenshot or mock-up, then a stock illustration, then generate one with POST /routine/content/image when nothing fits (blogs: feature plus inline, collections: one feature image in the main content). Use only live image URLs from guideline 25, library/images.json or that endpoint. Fetch each with curl first to confirm it returns 200 and is an image. Alt text 70 to 125 characters describing what the image shows. A feature image is used on one page only: check state.json (`feature_image`, `images`).
- Render and check: write the page to `pilot/<family>/<slug>.md`; `python3 tools/render.py <file> > /tmp/<slug>.resolved.md`; `python3 tools/lint.py <file>` must show no ERROR; `python3 tools/nightly_check.py state.json <file>` must show PASS. Fix and re-run, up to four rounds. If a page still fails, do NOT save it: skip the topic and say why in the report.
- Convert: blog `python3 tools/to_blogpost.py /tmp/<slug>.json /tmp/<slug>.resolved.md`; collection `python3 tools/to_collection.py /tmp/<slug>.json /tmp/<slug>.resolved.md`.
- Save: blog `curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data-binary @/tmp/<slug>.json https://api.carestreamai.com/routine/content/blog` (body is a JSON object `{"posts": [ ... ]}`: wrap the array that to_blogpost.py wrote); collection to `/routine/content/collections` with `{"collections": [ ... ]}`. A response with `created` or `updated` listing the slug means saved. `skipped` lists the reason otherwise (fix and retry once).
- After saving, add the new page to `state.json` in memory (slug, primary keyword, h2 headings, first twelve words, images) so the next page tonight is checked against it.

## Hard rules
- Drafts only. Never try to publish, feature or change a published page (the API refuses).
- Follow the house style: British English, no dashes in prose, no bold or italics, no banned phrases, no dates or years in prose, no raw prices (tokens only), no superlatives, no "CQC compliant" claims.
- If anything fails repeatedly (download, API errors), stop and report plainly. A night with two good pages is better than four weak ones.

## Final report (plain text)
For each page: title, slug, word count, lint and cross check result, claims cut, images used. Then: topics skipped and why, anything Len must decide.

## BLOG routine specifics
Topics: `pick_topics.py blog 4 state.json`. Each entry has format, voice, cluster, keywords and `verify_from` sources. Length per guideline 25 (900 to 2,000 words; aim for 1,300 to 1,800 unless the format needs less). Save at `pilot/<cluster>/<slug>.md`, slug `/blog/<slug>`.

## COLLECTION routine specifics
Topics: `pick_topics.py collection 6 state.json` (two training, two policy and two audit collections; when a kind has no topics left the others fill the night). Follow guidelines/10-collection-guideline.md exactly. The product grid is a fixed cluster of six products: read the cluster named in the topic entry in `ledger/collection-clusters.ts` (the six items are policy or training slugs) and the matching entries in `ledger/policy-catalogue.json` (policies), and describe the six products truthfully; if the cluster does not truly cover the topic, skip it and say so. Front matter must carry `kind` and `cluster_key`. Save at `pilot/<training|policies|audits>/<slug>.md`, slug `/collection/<slug>`.


## Collections: links and headings (added 18 Nov 2026)
Every collection must have, in the copy below the product grid, at least 3 different internal links (sitemap URLs, long tail descriptive anchors) and at least 2 different external links to primary sources (anchor names the document, URL fetched and confirmed), and a clean outline of real H2 and H3 headings (first heading H2, at least 2 H2 and 4 H3, no skipped levels, no fake headings). The prompt's older wording of two or three internal links is superseded. tools/lint.py fails the page if any of this is missing.


## Audit collections (added 24 Nov 2026)
An audits collection (kind: audits, family: audits) sells nothing: its six cards are FREE audits linking to /care-audits/<slug>. Read the cluster in ledger/collection-clusters.ts (AUDIT_CLUSTERS; the items are audit page slugs) and describe each audit from ledger/audit-catalogue.json and audits/page-copy/<slug>.json. Never claim an audit covers a service it is not tagged for (check its services in the catalogue); if the six do not truly fit the keyword, skip the topic and say so. Front matter: kind: audits, family: audits, cluster_key. Sample the format on pilot/audits/home-care-audits.md. Keywords must have Keyword Planner volume (the phrase 'domiciliary care audit' has none; use the nearby topic and form terms in the topic entry).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Resolve {{token}} placeholders from guidelines/product-facts.json. Usage: render.py file.md > out.md"""
import sys, json, re, os
facts = json.load(open(os.path.expanduser('~/carestream-content/guidelines/product-facts.json')))
text = open(sys.argv[1], encoding='utf-8').read()
missing = set()
def sub(m):
    k = m.group(1).strip()
    if k in facts: return facts[k]
    missing.add(k); return m.group(0)
out = re.sub(r'\{\{([^}]+)\}\}', sub, text)
sys.stdout.write(out)
if missing: sys.stderr.write('MISSING TOKENS: ' + ', '.join(sorted(missing)) + '\n')

{
  "version": 1,
  "updated": "2026-11-13",
  "rules": {
    "max_words": 60,
    "first_sentence_max_words": 25,
    "three_jobs": ["name the reader's situation or question", "give the answer or a clear promise within the first two sentences", "signal what is different about this page without relying on an unverified or niche detail"],
    "forbidden": ["[CHECK] or any unverified claim in the first 100 words", "calendar dates or years", "unexplained shorthand such as Standard 9 or Regulation 12(2)(h) before it is explained", "a summary of the article ('this guide explains...')"],
    "recency": "an opening type may not be used again until 8 other posts have used different types",
    "share_cap": "once there are 20 or more posts, no type may exceed 10 percent of them"
  },
  "moves": [
    {"id":"direct-answer","name":"Direct answer","job":"Answer the question in the first line, then say what follows.","fits":["G","B","E","collection"],"structure":"[answer in one sentence]. [one sentence on what the reader will find or be able to do].","examples":["Care homes do not have to run audits at a fixed interval, but they do have to show the ones they chose were enough. This page gives a rhythm to start from and the reasons to move it.","An infection prevention and control policy has to say who leads, what staff do each day and how an outbreak is handled. The headings below turn that into a policy you can read in one sitting."],"avoid":"Do not make it a definition of the topic. It must answer the question the page title asks.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"reader-moment","name":"The reader's moment","job":"Start in the situation the reader is in right now.","fits":["B","D","F","collection"],"structure":"[the moment, one concrete detail]. [the question it raises]. [one line promising what the page settles].","examples":["The new starter's first shift is tomorrow and the induction folder is still in the filing cabinet. Which of its contents do you actually need to hand over?","The inspection letter has arrived and the audit file is three months behind. Start with the pages that answer the first questions an inspector asks."],"avoid":"Do not reuse 'starts on Monday' or any fixed scene wording across pages. Vary the setting (residential, nursing, domiciliary, supported living) and the role.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"inspector-question","name":"The inspector's question","job":"Open with a question an inspector or auditor asks, then say what answers it.","fits":["C","G","collection"],"structure":"[the question, in the inspector's words]. [what a weak answer sounds like, one line]. [what the page gives instead].","examples":["Show me the last three times staff were told what changed in this policy. A manager who has to search for the answer has already told the inspector something.","Who is covering the lead's duties while they are on leave? The answer should be on one page, not in someone's head."],"avoid":"The question must be a real one the regulation or framework supports. No invented quotes attributed to named inspectors.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"consequence","name":"The consequence","job":"State what goes wrong if this is done badly.","fits":["F","D","B","E"],"structure":"[the failure, specific]. [why it happens]. [what the page offers to prevent it].","examples":["Two courses that cover different numbers of standards leave an assessor signing off work nobody can map. Choose the route with the records you will need at the end.","An audit that nobody owns produces findings that nobody closes. The fix is in who is named, not in the form."],"avoid":"No fear or urgency pressure. State the consequence plainly and move on to the help.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"common-mistake","name":"A common mistake","job":"Name one specific mistake services make, then correct it.","fits":["D","G","B","collection"],"structure":"[the mistake in one line]. [why it is easy to make]. [what to do instead, previewed].","examples":["Most services keep policies and hope they are current. The gap appears when a regulation changes and nobody rereads the document.","Auditing the form instead of the practice is the commonest way a good audit goes wrong."],"avoid":"Only use a mistake you can support from the regulations, official guidance or our product data. Never present a guess as common knowledge.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"product-number","name":"A number from our own product","job":"Open on a verified figure from CareStream that only we can give.","fits":["E","H","collection","F"],"structure":"[the figure, as a token if it can change]. [what it means for the reader]. [what the page does with it].","examples":["Four of the audits built into the library are daily. The rest run weekly, monthly, quarterly or at intervals you set, and that spread is the point.","Each course has thirty two questions and a pass mark. That tells you what a certificate on a record really shows."],"avoid":"Use a {{token}} for any number that can change. Never use a figure that is not in product-facts.json or verified in the product.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"thirty-second-test","name":"A 30 second self test","job":"Give the reader a quick check they can run immediately.","fits":["E","D","C","G"],"structure":"[three short things to check, as a sentence or a short list]. [what the result tells them]. [where the page goes next].","examples":["Pick one audit you run. When was the last one done, who signed it and what happened to the findings? If any answer takes more than a minute, read on.","Open your policy folder. Is there a review date, a named owner and a version number on each? Each missing item has a fix below."],"avoid":"Do not turn it into a quiz. Three checks at most.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"belief-corrected","name":"A belief to correct","job":"State a common wrong belief in one line, then correct it.","fits":["D","G"],"structure":"[the belief in the reader's own words]. [the correction in one sentence, with its source].","examples":["Holding a policy shows you are compliant. It shows you have a document. What an inspector tests is whether the people who work for you follow it.","An audit score is not a result. The actions that follow it are."],"avoid":"The correction must be verified. If it needs a source, name the source type in the text (the regulation, the guidance).","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"short-scene","name":"A short scene","job":"A few sentences that put the reader inside a moment.","fits":["A","B"],"structure":"[where and who, one sensory or concrete detail]. [what happens]. [the lesson the page draws out].","examples":["The cook has not been told which fridge the deputy will check first. That is deliberate, because a kitchen audit that is announced measures the announcement.","A care worker is easing a cardigan off a resident's shoulder and notices a mark that was not there yesterday. Nobody else is in the room."],"avoid":"Name the character and setting differently on every page. State once, in fresh words, that the scene is an illustration. No dates, no 'real case' boilerplate.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"plain-definition","name":"A plain English definition","job":"Define the thing in one clear sentence, then say why it matters.","fits":["H","G","collection"],"structure":"[X is Y, in plain words]. [the practical consequence for a service].","examples":["A kitchen audit is a set of questions asked on a visit, answered from what you see and what the records show. Every No becomes a task with an owner.","A safeguarding policy tells every member of staff what to do in the first five minutes after a concern."],"avoid":"No dictionary tone. The definition must be something a manager would nod at.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"the-decision","name":"The decision","job":"Frame the choice the reader has to make and the cost of choosing badly.","fits":["F"],"structure":"[the decision]. [the two or three things that should decide it]. [the promise of an answer].","examples":["You can pay once per learner or pay nothing per learner and carry the admin yourself. The better route depends on how many starters you take on in a year and who keeps the records.","Free for staff, free for the manager, or free but thin on records: the three routes differ less in cost than in what you can show afterwards."],"avoid":"Do not open with 'you need to choose'. Start from what makes the decision hard.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"ordinary-shift","name":"An ordinary shift","job":"Show where this matters on a normal working day.","fits":["B","A","C"],"structure":"[an ordinary moment on shift]. [what the policy, audit or course must make happen there]. [the page's route through it].","examples":["Half past two, handover is done and the afternoon is quiet. This is when a missed temperature check or an unread policy change goes unnoticed.","The late shift is two people short and a new starter is on the floor. What do they know, and where did they learn it?"],"avoid":"Keep it ordinary. No drama. Avoid clock times in headings (evergreen rule allows times of day but not dates).","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"paper-trail","name":"The paper trail","job":"Open on the evidence an inspector, commissioner or family could ask to see.","fits":["C","G","collection","E"],"structure":"[the record someone asks for]. [what it should show]. [how the page helps produce it].","examples":["When someone asks to see who passed, with what score and who watched them work, the answer should be one record, not three emails.","A policy review that happened but left no trace is, to an outsider, a review that did not happen."],"avoid":"Do not imply any record guarantees an outcome. Evidence supports a judgement, it does not decide it.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"trigger-moment","name":"A trigger moment","job":"Open on the event that sends people looking for this.","fits":["B","collection","F","E"],"structure":"[the trigger: a registration application, a new manager, a gap found, a contract request]. [what it demands]. [what the page provides].","examples":["A local authority contract asks for evidence of mandatory training for every member of staff. Most services can find it, but not quickly.","A new registered manager opens the policy folder and finds nothing has been reviewed since before they arrived. Start with the policies the regulations name."],"avoid":"The trigger must be one buyers genuinely face (inspection, registration, a contract, an incident, a change in law, a new manager). No fear lever.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"readers-question","name":"The reader's own question","job":"Open with the question as a manager would actually type or ask it.","fits":["G","B","collection","D"],"structure":"[the question in natural words]. [the short answer]. [what the page adds].","examples":["Do I really need a separate policy for every one of these? Not always, but the ones the regulations name each need a clear owner and a review date.","How many audits is enough? The regulations leave the number to you, and the page below helps you defend yours."],"avoid":"Use wording from real People Also Ask or search data, not a generic question. Do not stack two questions.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"surprising-verified-fact","name":"A verified, widely meaningful fact","job":"Open on a fact that surprises most readers and that we have verified.","fits":["G","D","E"],"structure":"[the fact]. [why it matters to a manager]. [the page's use of it].","examples":["The regulations set no fixed number of audits. They ask for systems that work, which is a harder standard than a number.","A certificate of completion and a signed-off competence are two different things, and an inspector can tell which one you hold."],"avoid":"Only if verified from a primary source in this draft. If it needs a [CHECK], choose another move.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"before-after","name":"Before and after","job":"Contrast how it works without this and with it.","fits":["B","F","collection"],"structure":"[the usual way, brief]. [the better way, brief]. [what the page shows].","examples":["Usually the audit lives in a binder and the actions live in someone's memory. Moving both into one place changes who checks what, and when.","Most services review a policy when it is old. A better trigger is a change in what staff are asked to do."],"avoid":"No disparagement of competitors or services. Describe habits, not people.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"small-numbers","name":"The small arithmetic","job":"Open with a simple calculation that makes the stakes concrete.","fits":["F","E","D"],"structure":"[the calculation in plain words]. [what the result means]. [what the page does about it].","examples":["A dozen starters a year means twelve records to chase and twelve certificates to match to people. The route you choose decides whether that is twelve minutes or twelve afternoons.","Eighteen monthly audits across a month is nearly one a working day. The schedule decides whether that is manageable."],"avoid":"Use numbers that are demonstrably true for the example. No invented statistics about the sector.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}},
    {"id":"what-it-is-not","name":"What it is not","job":"Clear a likely misunderstanding by saying what the thing is not.","fits":["G","H","D"],"structure":"[X is not Y]. [what it is, in one line]. [what follows].","examples":["The Care Certificate is not a qualification. It is a set of standards an employer observes and signs off, which changes what you ask of a course.","An audit is not a test of the staff. It is a test of whether the system works when the manager is not in the room."],"avoid":"The negation must be accurate and supported by official wording.","status":"active","weight":1.0,"stats":{"uses":0}}
  ]
}

# CareStream audit features (source for blog posts and collection pages)

Checked against the code on 2026-11-15. Each line: what it does, who has it. Blog angle ideas in brackets.

1. Completed-audit PDF report (every plan): branded PDF with overall and section scores, every answer with its CQC quality statement, photos, summary, action plan with outcomes and re-check results, and signatures. Saved against the run, emailed to admins. [how to prepare audit evidence for CQC; what a good audit report contains]
2. Photo evidence and signatures (every plan): per-question photos from the phone camera (annotatable), drawn signatures for the auditor and the manager. [using photo evidence in a care home audit]
3. Scheduling, reminders and escalation (every plan): assign an audit to a person with a due date and repeat; emails on assignment, 2 days before, when overdue, escalated to managers after a set number of days; admin summary daily or weekly. [how often to audit; stop audits being missed]
4. Manager approval (made available on every plan): a completed audit goes to the registered manager to approve or send back, with their name, date and signature recorded. [audit sign-off and accountability]
5. Action plans with closeout and re-check (manual actions every plan; AI-drafted plan on paid plans): owner, priority, due date, evidence photos, extensions, and the next audit shows last time's actions to re-check. [turning audit findings into an action plan]
6. Trends and repeat failures (every plan): score by month, repeat failures across consecutive audits, per-question trends. [spotting repeat failures before the inspector does]
7. CQC readiness score (paid plans, switched on in Settings): audit performance blended with policy coverage. [measuring inspection readiness]
8. WhatsApp audit flow: start and complete an audit by chat. [auditing from your phone]
9. Multi-site comparison (groups of 2 or more sites): side by side audit scores, repeat failures and overdue audits. [comparing homes in a group]
Also: 100+ free audits labelled by care service; every audit scored by section; conditional follow-up questions; CQC quality statement tags on questions; free to run on a free account; building your own, copying and AI import of existing audits are Enterprise.
