## Reasons

- cpd-eol-1: 1,000 plus 480 related searches at LOW competition (12 to 15); clear intent fit and a content gap beside the live training post.
- cpd-med-1: Medication competency (260) and assessment (110) at LOW competition (10 to 19); the collection lists 'medication competency assessment' as a secondary, so the template angle must stay informational and link to it.
- cpd-eol-2: 2,900 searches at competition index 0; legally sensitive so must be verified line by line; strong inspection-evidence angle.
- cpd-mh2-1: 8,100 'lolers' (grouped with LOLER, mixed industry traffic), LOW competition 27; six month inspection schedule is a clear gap in the live set.
- cpd-coshh-1: Highest informational demand in the set with LOW competition (index 26), but HSE and generic sites dominate; the care home angle (cleaning products, laundry, sluice) is the differentiator.
- cpd-hs-1: 18,100 at LOW competition (14); broad intent so aim at care manager duties; owner check clear, but HSE dominates the generic query.
- cpd-med-2: 1,900 and 3,600 related searches at LOW competition (13 and 0); clear worked example format.
- cpd-hs-2: 33,100 searches at competition index 2, but HSE owns the head term; the care home worked example is the realistic play.
- cpd-mh2-2: 1,300 at competition index 5; collection owns 'moving and handling training', so this regulation angle is clear.
- cpd-care-certificate-3: Planner returns 4,400 for the whole CPD phrase group (all professions, shared figure), so real care demand is far smaller; LOW to MEDIUM competition and strong trust fit across all ten courses.
- cpd-mh-1: Heavy generic demand (6,600 and 8,100 at LOW/MEDIUM competition) with a comparison angle; the live post owns the training term, so use the MHFA contrast only.
- cpd-coshh-2: 1,600 and 2,400 searches, MEDIUM competition; a template walkthrough fits the free audit product.
- cpd-ipc-1: 880 searches, MEDIUM 37; the audit draft already lists 'hand hygiene audit tool' as a secondary, so link rather than compete on that phrase.
- cpd-coshh-3: 320 searches but MEDIUM/HIGH competition and bids up to £6, so commercial pages crowd the results; informational answer on no legal expiry is the angle.
- cpd-gdpr-1: 210 searches at MEDIUM competition but CPC £2.74 to £9.90 shows heavy commercial pull; a certificate-question angle is distinct from the live GDPR training post.
- cpd-mh-3: 8,100 at competition 9 but generic awareness traffic; intent fit uncertain, so test with one page.
- cpd-care-certificate-2: 40 searches, competition index 11; high intent fit because it routes learners to genuine assessed practice. Close to the assessor draft, so keep it about the answers myth only.
- cpd-food-3: Very high volume but HIGH competition (74 to 83) and strongly commercial results (paid courses), so informational ranking is hard.
- cpd-food-1: 90 searches, competition index 5, but the live post already answers 'each year'; keep to a short expiry explainer or merge.
- cpd-ipc-2: 70 searches but HIGH competition (68) and the live post sits in the same space; consider as an update to that post.
- cpd-care-certificate-1: Low volume (30) but LOW competition; the owner page lists the exact phrase as a secondary, so write only as a distinct refresher explainer or fold into that page.
- cpd-food-2: 40,500 is mostly consumer lookups, so low intent fit; the kitchen audit pages own the care angle, so treat as a supporting link target only.
- cpd-hs-3: 70 searches, LOW competition but overlaps the live H&S awareness post; mark as supporting section.
- cpd-mh2-3: Every variant is 10 or fewer a month, but cluster demand is real; owner of 'manual handling certificate' is the collection, avoid that phrase.
- cpd-gdpr-2: Only 20 searches and the policy collection owns the GDPR policy set; low priority, a candidate for a section in the collection instead.
- cpd-med-3: Primary has no data and collection owns 'medication training'; low priority.
- cpd-gdpr-3: Primary has no data and the broader 'gdpr training' (880, HIGH/MEDIUM) belongs to the live post; use only if the live post is revised.
- cpd-ipc-3: No Planner data; only worthwhile if Search Console shows demand.
- cpd-eol-3: No data for the long tail, primary stem 'end of life care training' (140) belongs to the live post; only worth doing as a section added to that post.
- cpd-mh-2: 10 searches; only a supporting page.

# Competitors that give away what CareStream gives away free (18 Nov 2026)

What CareStream gives free on every plan: CPD certified training (Care Certificate and annual refreshers), 100+ care audit templates, and screening of the first 5 policies. Paid: AI answers, gap fixes, translation, incentives, resident profiles and the rest.

Method: six web searches on 18 Nov 2026 (the search tool is US based, so UK ranking order is not reliable; the earlier UK Google results from Len's Chrome are in serp-intel-uk-2026-11-13.md). Everything below is vendor marketing until checked on the page. Nothing here is a verified claim about a competitor and none of it may be quoted as fact in published content.

## Tier 1: give a free version AND sell a paid platform (the closest threat)
| Competitor | What is free | Paid / notes |
|---|---|---|
| Caredemy (caredemy.co.uk) | Free CPD care course set; claims CPD Standards Office and Skills for Care endorsement | 160+ courses and the Care Certificate behind a subscription |
| GoAudits (goaudits.com) | 5 free CQC self assessment templates (one per quality question) as PDF or app; audit schedule PDF; training matrix template | 40+ care audit templates and the platform behind a free trial |
| AlwaysReady Care (always-ready-care.web.app) | Free tier: evidence capture, 5 templates, compliance dashboard, 3 staff logins | Pro from about 79 pounds per home per month |
| Log my Care (logmycare.co.uk) | Free CQC inspection checklist PDF; markets "free care home software" | Paid care management platform |
| Florence (florence.co.uk) | Free training matrix and competency framework templates; care home essentials pack | Paid shifts and care platform; bids on the same search ads |
| Careskills Academy | "Free Care Certificate, 1 course and 1 portfolio" | Paid catalogue |
| Caring for Care (caringforcare.co.uk) | Courses from 2 pounds plus VAT; audit tool guidance content | Paid catalogue and tools |
| The Mandatory Training Group, HL Online Training, Learn for Care | Free care courses or free Care Certificate offers (from the 13 Nov UK results) | Paid course catalogues |

## Tier 2: free public or sector bodies (set the expectation that it is free)
NHS England eLfH (free Care Certificate e-learning, the 16 standards), Skills for Care (standards, matrix guidance), Care England SMART audit tool (free, aligned to the CQC Single Assessment Framework, unverified), Bolton Council (published training framework and matrix), Lancashire County Council (infection control audit PDF), Local Government Association (self assessment workbook, councils not providers), Digital Care Hub.

## Tier 3: paid incumbents that rank for the same keywords
QCS, The Access Group (130+ policies and a blog arguing free software lacks compliance depth), Birdie, Croner-i, OnCare (policy templates), Care4Quality, Worknest, CloudAssess (training matrix and blog content), Learning Curve Group (funded qualifications), Reed (listed Care Certificate bundles).

## Tier 4: free no sign up tools that compete for the same search terms
Teamz Lab (tool.teamzlab.com): free CQC Inspection Readiness Checker and Compliance Score Calculator, no signup. Lumiform, SafetyCulture and Jotform: generic mock inspection templates. High Speed Training (free CQC inspection checklist, a content marketing hub).

## Gaps and notes already seen
- No result showed a fully free complete CQC policy pack for care homes: free items were single policies (Care4Quality Freedom to Speak Up) or samples. CareStream's free policy screening of 5 policies looks unusual.
- NHS England eLfH already gives the Care Certificate free, so CareStream must never claim to be the only free route (already in the 13 Nov research).
- Many pages still say 15 Care Certificate standards; the March 2025 update made it 16.

## Proposed research per competitor
Blog and resource sitemap, titles and H1/H2 outline of each post, the free offer pages, pricing page headings (never copy prices into our content), the keywords in titles and URLs. Then: topic gaps against our ledger, Keyword Planner volumes for each gap, scored and added to the topic backlog for Len to approve.

# CareStream scenario pages: ideas and creation template (18 Nov 2026)

Status: ideas only. Nothing here is in the nightly lists. Len approves scenarios first, then keyword research runs per scenario, then pages are written.

A scenario page = one real situation a provider, manager or owner is in, one objection or pain, and how CareStream is used in that situation. Every step must be a feature the platform really has today (checked against reference_carestream_audit_features and the live product). Anything not yet built is marked [CHECK] and is not written until confirmed.

## The pattern (from the face to face example)
1. The objection or situation, in the buyer's own words.
2. The honest question that exposes the gap ("can you say every carer understood it?").
3. How CareStream fills the gap, step by step, using real features.
4. What the manager can now show (evidence for CQC, the owner, the family).
5. What it does not do (stated plainly, builds trust).

## A. Objections and "we already do X"
1. "We still want face to face training": CareStream complements it, follow up questions check retention, in the carer's own language. (Len's example)
2. "We already use another training provider": run the free CPD alongside to fill gaps and show what staff actually retained.
3. "We have a paper policy folder": screen the first 5 policies free, see gaps against regulations.
4. "We already do audits on paper or spreadsheets": move to the audit library with scoring and actions.
5. "Our staff are not good with computers": phone based, short lessons, language choice. [CHECK device and login flow]
6. "We cannot afford training time": short lessons in small gaps in the shift. [CHECK lesson lengths]
7. "Free means poor quality": the CPD certification, who certified it, what free covers on every plan.
8. "We have a consultant who writes our policies": use screening to check the consultant's policies against the regulations.
9. "Our manager does all of this in their head": evidence trail so the knowledge is not one person.
10. "We passed CQC last time, we are fine": what changed since (Single Assessment Framework, Care Certificate 16 standards).

## B. Language and communication
11. Staff whose first language is not English: training in their language.
12. International recruits in their first weeks: induction plus Care Certificate in their language.
13. Checking understanding after a safeguarding talk in a team meeting.
14. Handover instructions that must be understood the same way by everyone. [CHECK]
15. A mixed language team where one carer always translates for the others.
16. Policy changes: proving that every member of staff, in any language, has understood the new version. [CHECK translation of policies]

## C. Training and competence
17. New starter on day one: what they do in week one, what the manager sees.
18. Annual refresher season: 40 staff, one deadline, no chasing.
19. Care Certificate for a service that has never run it.
20. Agency or bank staff who arrive with certificates you cannot verify. [CHECK agency flows]
21. A carer who passed a course but made a medication error: closing the loop with targeted retraining.
22. Linking an audit failure to the free course that fixes it.
23. Training matrix for an inspection: who is in date, who is not.
24. Staff who do the training at home, unpaid: how to make time visible.
25. Preparing staff for a mock inspection conversation.
26. Moving and handling refresher after a near miss.
27. Infection control refresher after an outbreak.
28. Dementia awareness for night staff.
29. Fire safety evidence for a fire officer visit.
30. Safeguarding: a concern was raised, was everyone trained?

## D. Inspection and audit
31. CQC announces a visit tomorrow: the 24 hour evidence check.
32. A new registered manager in their first 30 days.
33. After a "requires improvement": a 90 day recovery plan built from audits.
34. Preparing for a local authority commissioner visit.
35. Monthly manager audit routine in 2 hours.
36. Deputy covering while the manager is on leave.
37. Owner of three homes wanting one view of all three.
38. Audit finding to action to re-audit, with proof of closure.
39. Medication audit after a controlled drug discrepancy.
40. Mealtime audit after a complaint about food.
41. Falls audit after a cluster of falls.
42. Environment audit before the fire risk assessment review.
43. Bed rail safety check after a CQC alert or notice.
44. Care plan audit sample for a resident of the day.
45. Infection prevention audit before winter.
46. Custom audit: a provider builds their own for a specialist service. [CHECK custom audits]

## E. Policies
47. A new policy needed after an incident: from gap to published policy.
48. Policy review cycle: which of your policies are out of date.
49. A policy that names your service and leads, not a generic template.
50. Missing policy flow: spotting a policy you did not know you needed. [CHECK]
51. Mental Capacity Act and DoLS policy review after the LPS change.
52. Whistleblowing: does every carer know who to call?
53. Duty of candour after something went wrong.
54. Data protection: ICO registration, retention, subject access request.
55. Setting specific policies (domiciliary, supported living, nursing).

## F. People, retention and culture
56. Staff incentives: monthly points campaigns for training done and audits completed. [CHECK phase 1 live]
57. Carers who feel unrecognised: turning compliance into recognition.
58. High turnover: what the first 90 days should look like.
59. Supervision and appraisal evidence.
60. Staff who want a career: CPD certificates they keep.

## G. Residents and families
61. "This is me" resident profiles: new resident, agency carer, no key worker on shift. [CHECK profile fields]
62. Person centred care plan sitting next to a profile of likes and routines.
63. A new carer meeting a resident with dementia on the first day.
64. Family asks "do you know my mum?": showing person centred practice.
65. Night staff covering a unit they rarely work.

## H. Business and owners
66. Owner who is not clinical wanting proof things are running.
67. Registered manager leaving: keeping evidence and knowledge in the service.
68. Selling or buying a home: due diligence evidence.
69. Insurance renewal: showing training and audit records.
70. Commissioner or local authority contract tender: evidence pack.
71. New provider registering with CQC for the first time.
72. Group with a head office compliance lead.

## I. Setting based (the same pattern for each service)
73. Residential care home. 74. Nursing home. 75. Domiciliary care. 76. Supported living. 77. Learning disability service. 78. Mental health service. 79. Dementia specialist unit. 80. Children's home [CHECK scope]. Dentistry, GP and hospital pages only once those policy waves exist.

## Suggested first batch (strongest fit, likely search or ad demand)
Face to face follow up (1), language (11, 12, 16), annual refresher deadline (18), CQC visit tomorrow (31), recovery plan after requires improvement (33), audit failure to training (22), new manager first 30 days (32), "we already have paper policies" (3), staff incentives (56), "This is me" for agency staff (61).

# Scenario page creation template

Each scenario is one file in research/scenarios/<slug>.md, filled in this order. Stage 1 to 3 happen BEFORE any writing.

## Stage 1: Scenario brief
- Slug and working title (plain, no dashes):
- Audience (role and setting): owner, registered manager, deputy, training lead, compliance lead, commissioner
- Trigger moment: what happened that made them search or object
- The objection or pain in their own words (use real client wording, remove names):
- The honest question (the one that exposes the gap):
- Outcome they want:

## Stage 2: Keyword research (required, gate before drafting)
1. Seed terms: the buyer's wording for the trigger, the pain, and the outcome (at least 10 phrasings, including how a manager would type it into Google, not our product words).
2. Pull ideas and UK volumes with the keyword planner tools (keyword_ideas then keyword_volumes). Record volume, competition and date.
3. Check the SERP in Len's Chrome (UK): who ranks, which page type (guide, template, product, forum), what the top 3 do not answer.
4. Intent check: informational (blog), comparison, or commercial (collection or product). Commercial terms go to collections per the collections rule, not scenario pages.
5. Cluster: list related questions and long tails that belong on this one page.
6. Pick one primary keyword, 3 to 6 secondary, and 3 or more questions for H3s.
7. Decision gate:
   - Primary volume 50 or more: write as a search page.
   - Volume under 50 but strategically strong (sales objection, ad landing, email, sales call): write as a sales or ad scenario page, noindex decision recorded, do not chase search.
   - No demand and no strategic use: drop it.
8. Overlap check against existing posts, collections, /uses/ pages and policy product head terms (never target a paid policy keyword).
9. Save: primary, secondary, volumes, date, SERP notes, decision. Add volumes to the backlog so the highlighter shows them.

## Stage 3: Feature and fact check
- List every platform feature the scenario uses. Each must be live and verified. Mark the screen or flow it comes from.
- List every legal or regulator claim. Each needs a primary source (legislation.gov.uk, CQC, NHS England, HSE, ICO, Skills for Care) fetched and logged in the claims log.
- Anything not live is removed or marked [CHECK] and the page waits.
- Never state competitor prices or unverified competitor claims.

## Stage 4: Page structure
1. H1 containing the primary keyword, in the buyer's words.
2. Opening: the situation in two or three sentences, then the honest question.
3. H2 "What usually happens" (the gap, without blaming the manager).
4. H2 "How CareStream is used here": numbered steps, each a real feature, with a real screenshot or accurate mock-up per the accuracy rule.
5. H2 "What you can show afterwards": the evidence (a report, the matrix, a score, a history).
6. H2 "What this does not do": plain limits.
7. H2 questions as H3s from the keyword research, each with a direct answer first.
8. FAQ (3 to 5 from the questions).
9. Call to action: the free route first (free CPD, free audits, first 5 policies screened), then paid features if the scenario needs them.
- Internal links: at least 3 (product, collection, related scenarios). External links: at least 2 primary sources. Descriptive anchors only.
- H2 and H3 only, first heading H2.

## Stage 5: Style and rules
- British English. No em or en dashes. Plain words. Light design.
- Never claim CareStream is the only free route (NHS England eLfH exists).
- Care Certificate is 16 standards.
- Images: feature image once, never repeated in the body; people with open visible eyes; product images only real screenshots or accurate mock-ups.
- Do not name real clients or staff. Use composite or invented names marked as examples.

## Stage 6: Checks and publish
- lint.py passes, claims log written, volumes recorded, cross check passes.
- Draft only. Len reviews, then publishes.
- After publish: add to the sitemap automatically, add internal links from related pages, record in the ledger.

## Where scenario pages live (to decide)
Option 1: the existing /uses/ section. Option 2: blog posts with a scenario format. Option 3: a new /scenarios/ section with a hub page. Recommendation: a hub at /scenarios/ with each page linking to the matching product and collection, so they work as sales pages and as search pages.

# UK live search results, 13 November 2026 (Google UK, from Len's Chrome)

Method: google.co.uk, hl=en, gl=uk. Results are what one UK searcher saw. Treat claims as marketing snippets until verified on the page.

## free care certificate
Top organic: Caredemy (free CPD care courses), NHS England care-certificate page, The Mandatory Training Group (free care courses), eLFH Care Certificate (CCT) programme, HL Online Training (free Care Certificate in a library subscription, still says "15 standards"), Skills for Care standards, Florence (Pathway to Care: 11 free courses and free certificates, 8 to 10 hours), Skills for Health, My Free Courses (funded Level 2, 19+).
Ads: Free Courses In England, Alison, The AIM Group, Florence, Learn for Care.
AI Overview says: free training materials for the 16 standards are on the NHS England eLfH hub; the Care Certificate is an induction set of standards, not a regulated qualification; the employer signs it off after observing practical skills.
People also ask: Can I do the care certificate online for free? How much does it cost to get a care certificate? How do I get my care certificate? Which certificate can I do online for free?
Related: free care certificate online, free care certificate nhs, free care certificate courses uk, how to get a care certificate nhs online, care certificate online, care certificate course, elfh care certificate, care certificate pdf free download.
IMPORTANT: NHS England eLfH already provides free e-learning for the Care Certificate. Our page must NOT claim to be the only free route. Our real difference is on the employer side: CPD certified course, assessment, certificates, training matrix, unlimited staff accounts, records for CQC evidence, no card.

## care certificate standards
AI Overview: 16 standards since the March 2025 update (Skills for Care, NHS England, Skills for Health). Added: Awareness of learning disability and autism. Standards listed: Understand your role; Your personal development; Duty of care; Equality, diversity, inclusion and human rights; Work in a person-centred way; Communication; Privacy and dignity; Fluids and nutrition; Awareness of mental health and dementia; Adult safeguarding; Safeguarding children; Basic life support; Health and safety; Handling information; Infection prevention and control; Awareness of learning disability and autism. (VERIFY against the Skills for Care document before publishing.)
Also stated: not in statute; CQC expects it as part of safe induction (the AI overview ties it to Regulation 18, VERIFY).
Top organic: Skills for Care standards page and PDFs, NHS England care-certificate page ("based on 16 standards"), tri.x (still says 15), Skills for Health, The Access Group (still says 15), People Alchemy (16, April 2025), Academy for Health & Fitness (16, Jan 2026).
People also ask: What are the 15 standards of the Care Certificate? What are the 16 standards? What are the 5 care standards? Is it a legal requirement to have a care certificate?
Related: free 15 care certificate standards, what are the 16 care certificate standards, nhs care certificate standards, care certificate standards workbook, workbook pdf free download, care certificate standards 2026, standards pdf, standards 2021.
GAP: many pages still say 15 standards. A clear, correct 16 standard explainer with the 2025 change is valuable.

## care home audit template
Top organic: Caring For Care (free PDF checklist), GoAudits (40+ templates, CQC SAF aligned), Infection Prevention Control (monthly audit tool PDF), Wirral NHS trust IPC audit tools, ModernGov Wolverhampton (quality assurance self-assessment), W&P Compliance Centre, Dignity in Care, NHS Cornwall and Isles of Scilly care home resources.
Ads: QCS (care home audit tool), Croner-i, The Access Group.
AI Overview groups audits by frequency: medication monthly; care plans and risk assessments monthly or quarterly; infection prevention and control monthly; health, safety and environment monthly or quarterly; safeguarding and dignity quarterly; HR, recruitment and training annual or ongoing.
People also ask: What audits need to be done in a care home? What are the 5 C's of audit? What not to say during an audit? What are the 7 steps in the audit process?
Related: free domiciliary care audit template, free care home audits, infection control audit template, care plan audit template, ipc audit checklist, domiciliary care audits.
Also seen: GoAudits "Which Care Home Audits Are Mandatory, and How Often?" and "care home audit schedule".

## care home kitchen audit
AI Overview: covers temperature control (fridge, freezer, hot holding, probe calibration), hygiene and cleaning sign off, allergen labelling and stock rotation, COSHH and chemicals, equipment and pests, mealtime experience. Points to the Food Standards Agency Safer Food Better Business and the Malnutrition Task Force meal time audit tool.
Top organic: welcometoable.co.uk (kitchen hygiene checklist), Mitti (kitchen audit template, HACCP), ASL Catering (CQC inspection kitchen checklist, 29 Jul 2026), Malnutrition Task Force (meal time experience audit tool PDF), GoAudits (care home kitchen audit), GOV.UK (Safer food, better business supplement for residential care homes, 25 Jun 2026), Centrim Life (kitchen audits, weekly and monthly), AbleCare Kitchens (CQC FSMS guide), Checkit.
Ads: QCS, Peninsula, Food Alert, Avensure.
People also ask: What audits need to be done in a care home? How often should a kitchen audit take place? What happens if you fail a kitchen inspection? How often are care homes audited?
Related: care home kitchen audit checklist, safer food better business, SFBB pack, haccp, food standards agency.

## what policies does a care home need
Top organic: CQC fundamental standards page, W&P Compliance Centre (residential care home policies), InspectReady (every CQC required policy list, 28 Mar 2026), Care Sync Experts, Affinity Care Advisory ("what policies does a care home need", 8 May 2025), Croner-i (required and recommended policies table), CareBound (policies checklist, 6 Dec 2025), QCS, Infection Prevention Control (30 IPC guidance documents).

| resident of the day checklist | 20 | Low (0) | Audit template page |
| bed rail safety checklist | 10 | Low (0) | Audit template page (GoAudits has one) |
| dols checklist / mental capacity act audit care home | 10 / n/a | Low | Pair with the DoLS explainer |
| mock cqc inspection cost | 10 | Medium (57) | Pricing intent: be careful, never state competitor prices |

## D. Care planning (ties to the new Resident profiles, "This is me")
| Keyword | Volume | Competition | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| person centred care plan example | 170 | Low (4) | Strong fit: how a profile of likes, routines and life story sits beside the care plan, without clinical content |
| consent in care | 50 | Low (1) | Possible, mind the legal accuracy |

## E. Setting and recruitment (smaller, later)
cqc registration requirements (210, Medium 65, audience mostly new providers), right to work checks for agency staff (n/a), domiciliary care mandatory training (10, High), reporting incidents care home (n/a), incident report form template (n/a).

## F. Rejected as off audience or off topic
Consumer dementia care terms (how to care for someone with dementia 140, understanding dementia 210), leave and rota templates, LMS and software terms, Australia and Ireland compliance, ADHD or autism treatment, white label CPD courses.

## Quiz pages (a competitor pattern, low volume)
Caring for Care publishes many "quiz with answers" pages (safeguarding, manual handling, infection control, complaint handling, first aid). Keyword Planner shows 10 or less each, so volume is tiny, but together they build topical depth. Consider only if we can use our own CPD assessment questions, never theirs.

## What the competitors do NOT cover (the gap that is ours)
- No audit library with scoring and actions (GoAudits gates its templates behind a 14 day trial).
- No free policy screening or policy gap check at all.
- No free CPD certified core courses linked to audit findings. Caredemy's free set is management and CQC topics; Caring for Care has quiz certificates; HL ties its free Care Certificate to a paid subscription.
- Thin regulation by regulation guides (only GoAudits touches Reg 15 and 17).
- Setting specific audits (dentistry, GP, hospitals, mental health) barely covered.

## Caveats
Competitor claims are from their own marketing pages and unverified. Some titles were taken from URL slugs. Post counts are lower bounds (truncated sitemaps). Never copy their text or state their prices. Volumes are small across this niche, so the head terms in section A matter most.

# Free audits to add: master plan (from the six research files in this folder)
14 November 2026. Research only. 81 audit proposals across six service groups; after removing the ones that repeat across groups, about 60 distinct audits. Volumes are Keyword Planner UK per month; most "<name> audit" phrases are under 10, so demand sits on form and template words and the case rests on what regulators expect.

## What the competitors do that our audit tool does not (build these first, they unlock many audits)
1. Scope units beyond resident, room and staff member: per client visit (home care), per person file, per child, per record or radiograph, per equipment item, per placement.
2. Percentage scoring with re-audit cycles and trends over time.
3. An action owner, due date and follow up audit for every "No" answer.
4. A schedule: weekly, monthly, quarterly, rolling (Resident of the Day, 3 monthly spot checks).
5. Every audit mapped to a CQC key question and regulation (or the Ofsted standard).

Researched 2026-11-14. Research only, nothing live. No question text copied from any source; titles, scope sentences, frequencies and URLs only.

Volumes are UK monthly searches from Keyword Planner (see section 5). Demand for this group is very small; this is a coverage and trust play, not a traffic play.

| 8 | Antimicrobial Prescribing Audit | Dental, private GP | Gap | Two cycles a year (re-audit after change) | Per prescription (sample) | Reg 12(2)(g),(h) | Medium |
| 9 | Sharps, Inoculation Injury and Clinical Waste Audit | Dental, clinics, hospitals | Gap | Quarterly | Whole service | Reg 12(2)(h), Reg 15 | Medium |
| 10 | Dental Unit Waterline and Legionella Audit | Dental | Close: Water Safety and Legionella needs a dental version | Monthly checks, annual review | Per dental unit | Reg 12(2)(h), Reg 15 | Medium |
| 11 | Clinical Equipment, Servicing and Validation Audit | All three groups | Close: Premises and Maintenance does not cover clinical equipment or validation | Quarterly | Per item of equipment | Reg 15, Reg 12(2)(e) | Medium |
| 12 | Vaccine and Medicines Fridge (Cold Chain) Audit | Clinics and private GP, hospitals, dental | Gap | Daily log, monthly review | Per fridge | Reg 12(2)(g) | Low |
| 13 | Patient Access and Disability Access Audit | Dental, clinics | Gap | Annual | Whole service | Reg 15, Reg 10, Equality Act context (not fetched) | Low |

Also considered but not recommended as stand-alone audits: Complaints audit (we have Monthly Governance Review and Resident Feedback Round; make a patient version of those), Controlled Drugs audit (fold into a clinic/hospital variant of Medicines Management), Sepsis/deteriorating patient and VTE audits (hospital only, near zero search demand, defer until a hospital-specific phase), Theatre cleaning (defer with hospital phase).

### Detail for each recommended audit

Sections are headings only.

1. **Dental Decontamination (HTM 01-05) Audit**. Dental practices (also relevant to any clinic that reprocesses instruments). Scope: how instruments move through cleaning, inspection, sterilisation, storage and traceability, and whether equipment is validated. Sections: Decontamination room layout and dirty to clean flow; Cleaning and washer-disinfector use; Sterilisers and validation records; Packaging, storage and shelf life; Traceability and records; Training and competence; Actions. Frequency six-monthly. Scope whole service. Evidences Reg 12(2)(h) and Reg 17. Confirmed as normal by: NHS England and Infection Prevention Society dental audit tool, CQC dental mythbusters on decontamination, BDA infection control audit, GoAudits, SafetyCulture. Priority High: the single most-cited dental audit, CQC expects it every six months.
2. **Dental Radiography Quality and Justification Audit**. Dental, plus clinics and hospitals with X-ray. Scope: whether each exposure was justified, reported and of acceptable quality, and the QA programme is current. Sections: Justification and authorisation; Image quality grading; Reporting and clinical evaluation; Dose and diagnostic reference level comparison; Equipment QA and servicing; Staff training and roles; Actions. Quarterly sample, yearly programme review. Per radiograph. Evidences IR(ME)R 2017 reg 7 (clinical audit in employer's procedures). Sources: BDA radiograph quality audit, SDCEP radiology QA and audit example, GoAudits radiograph template, RQIA and NI dental IR(ME)R guidance. High: named in legislation, 20 searches a month for the exact term, highest of the dental specifics.
3. **Clinical Record Keeping Audit**. All. Scope: sampled patient records for completeness, legibility, justification and follow up. Sections: Identification and history; Examination and findings; Diagnosis, options and plan; Consent and communication; Prescribing and referrals; Follow up and recall; Actions. Quarterly, per record. Evidences Reg 17(2)(c). Sources: BDA record keeping template, FGDP(UK) clinical examination and record keeping guidance and audits built on it, NHS Wales dental clinical audit examples, SafetyCulture Medical Audit Checklist, GoAudits dental record audit. High: appears in every competitor list.
4. **Hand Hygiene Observation Audit**. All. Scope: observed hand hygiene at the key moments for each role. Sections: Facilities and supplies; Observed technique; Moments of care; Bare below elbow and PPE; Staff feedback; Actions. Monthly, per staff member observed. Reg 12(2)(h). Sources: CQC dental mythbuster 9 hand hygiene (title seen in search; page not fetched), SDCEP infection prevention content, GoAudits hygiene templates. High: 140 searches a month, the largest real demand in this group, and generalises across every service.
5. **Medical Emergencies and Resuscitation Readiness Check**. Sections: Emergency drugs and expiry; Oxygen and airway kit; AED and defibrillator; Staff training and rehearsal; Accessible location and signage; Incident review; Actions. Weekly or monthly, whole service. Reg 12(2)(b),(c),(e). Sources: SDCEP practice support manual (topic seen in search), SafetyCulture and Lumiform healthcare equipment checks; only 10 searches a month. High because it is a regulator staple and cheap to build.
6. **Consent and Information Sharing Audit**. Sections: Capacity and understanding; Information given; Written consent for procedures; Consent to share with NHS GP; Children and young people; Actions. Quarterly, per record. Reg 11. CQC report on independent doctors and clinics found poor sharing with NHS GPs (reported by trade press, CQC pages 403). Medium.
7. **WHO Surgical Safety Checklist Observation Audit**. Private hospitals. Sections: Sign in; Time out; Sign out; Team engagement; Records; Actions. Monthly, per procedure observed. Reg 12. Evidence: CQC independent hospital inspection reports (e.g. London Welbeck and Priory Hospital reports surfaced in search) criticised record-only checks and praised monthly observational audits. Medium.
8. **Antimicrobial Prescribing Audit**. Sections: Indication recorded; Agent, dose and duration; Alternatives and advice; Follow up; Comparison to guideline; Actions. Two cycles, per prescription. Source: NHS England Midlands dental audit page (fetched). Medium.
9. **Sharps, Inoculation Injury and Clinical Waste Audit**. Sections: Sharps handling and safer devices; Disposal containers; Inoculation injury process; Waste segregation; Storage and collection; Training. Quarterly, whole service. BDA lists a healthcare waste audit (seen on public BDA listing via search). Medium.
10. **Dental Unit Waterline and Legionella Audit**. Sections: Water source and treatment; Flushing routine; Disinfection regimen; Testing and results; Risk assessment; Actions. Monthly checks, per dental unit. Source: CQC dental mythbuster 5 on dental waterline management (title seen in search). Medium.
11. **Clinical Equipment, Servicing and Validation Audit**. Sections: Inventory; Service and calibration dates; Validation records; Faults and repair; User training; Actions. Quarterly, per item. CQC mythbuster 12 on validation of decontamination equipment (title seen in search). Medium.
12. **Vaccine and Medicines Fridge (Cold Chain) Audit**. Sections: Fridge and thermometer; Daily min and max log; Out of range response; Stock rotation; Power failure plan. Daily log, monthly review, per fridge. Low: 10 to 20 searches a month and HIGH competition on the checklist term.
13. **Patient Access and Disability Access Audit**. Sections: Entrance and routes; Reception and waiting; Treatment room access; Communication needs; Adjustments log. Annual, whole service. 110 searches a month for "disability access audit" (generic, not healthcare), BDA lists a disability access audit. Low.

## 2. Structural features competitors have that we may lack

(From the public pages that loaded; confirm against our product.)
- Cycle based audit and re-audit: NHS England dental audit pages describe data collection, improvement period, then second cycle against a standard. We should support "re-audit linked to the first".
- Sampling (per record, per radiograph, per prescription) rather than per resident.
- Observational audits of staff practice (hand hygiene, WHO checklist) with per-staff scoring; CQC reports reject record only checks.
- Scoring and percentage compliance, an action plan with owners and dates, and a record of audit sheet (SDCEP Record of Audit template).
- Non-conformance and CAPA forms (SafetyCulture Smartclinic).
- Per equipment and per dental unit scope.

## 4. Section outlines (headings only)

1. Care Worker Spot Check: Visit arrival and identity; Communication and dignity; Care plan tasks followed; Medication and records; Infection control and PPE; Moving and handling; Feedback from client and actions.
2. MAR Chart Audit: Client and MAR details; Entries and signatures; Codes, gaps and missed doses; Allergies and prescriber changes; PRN and topical records; Match to care plan and daily notes; Actions.
3. Medication Competency Assessment: Training and knowledge; Observed administration; Prompting versus administering; Recording; Errors and escalation; Sign-off and review date.
4. Daily Care Notes Audit: Visit completeness; Person-centred detail; Changes in condition escalated; Consent and capacity; Legibility and timeliness; Match to care plan; Actions.
5. Late and Missed Visit Review: Visit log summary; Late and missed visits by reason; Time-critical visits (medication, meals); Client impact and follow-up; Travel and rota patterns; Trends and actions.
6. Home Environment Risk Review: Access and security; Hazards and falls; Fire, gas and electrics; Equipment in the home; Hygiene and pests; Pets and other occupants; Actions agreed with client.
7. Lone Working and Safety: Risk assessments in place; Check-in and escalation; Travel and out-of-hours; Aggression and safeguarding of staff; Training and kit; Incident review.
8. Moving and Handling: Assessment current; Equipment inspection and servicing; Technique observed; Worker training; Client views; Changes and actions.
9. Supervision and Appraisal Records: Schedule and compliance; Content and quality; Observed practice linked; Learning and development; Wellbeing; Actions.
10. Complaints and Compliments: Log completeness; Acknowledgement and timescales; Investigation quality; Outcome and learning; Duty of candour link; Trends.
11. Home Care Infection and PPE: PPE supply and use; Hand hygiene; Handling waste and laundry in homes; Cleaning of shared equipment; Outbreak and illness reporting; Training.
12. Mental Capacity and Consent: Consent recorded; Capacity assessments decision-specific; Best-interest records; LPA and representatives; Restrictions in the home; Review.
13. Live-in Placement Review: Carer rest breaks and hours; Rotation and handover; Client wellbeing and activities; Home and equipment; Records and medication; Relief cover and escalation; Carer welfare.
14. Business Continuity and Emergency Cover: Plan current; Priority client list; Staffing shortfall and weather; IT and call-system failure; Contact trees; Test and review.

### Detail per audit (sections headings only)

1. **Ligature & Environmental Risk Audit.** Scope: anchor points, fittings and ward environment for self-harm risk. Sections: Entrances and communal areas; Bedrooms and bathrooms; Courtyards and outside space; Fixtures, furniture and fittings; Observation lines and blind spots; Action plan and re-audit. Sources: CQC MHA monitoring (environment page, 403 to fetch, search snippet only); CCQI AIMS environment audit.
2. **Restrictive Practice, Restraint & Seclusion Review.** Scope: each use of restraint, seclusion, segregation reviewed for necessity and proportionality. Sections: Incident and trigger; Least restrictive alternatives; Authorisation and recording; Monitoring and post-incident support; Debrief and learning; Patient and family involvement. Sources: CQC MHA reviewer reports (seclusion/long-term segregation section).
3. **Rapid Tranquillisation & Physical Health Monitoring.** Sections: Prescribing and indication; Administration; Post-dose observations; Escalation; Debrief; Learning.
4. **MHA Legal Compliance.** Sections: Detention papers and authority; Rights explained; Consent to treatment and capacity; Section 17 leave authorisation; Nearest relative/IMHA; Tribunal and manager hearings.
5. **Controlled Drugs Audit.** Sections: Storage and keys; Register entries and balances; Ordering and receipt; Administration and witnessing; Destruction and returns; Incidents and accountable officer.
6. **Syringe Driver & Anticipatory Medicines.** Sections: Prescription and indication; Set-up and checks; Monitoring and site; Documentation; Stock and storage; Incidents.
7. **Advance Care Planning & DNACPR.** Sections: Identification of need; Conversation and capacity; Recording of wishes; DNACPR decision quality; Review and sharing; Out of hours availability.
8. **End of Life Care Pathway.** Sections: Recognition of dying; Individual care plan; Symptom control; Communication with family; Care after death; Review.
9. **Detox & Withdrawal Monitoring.** Sections: Assessment and risk; Prescribing; Withdrawal scales and observations; Escalation; Nutrition/thiamine and physical health; Discharge and harm reduction.
10. **OST, Take-home & Naloxone.** Sections: Prescription and dispensing; Supervised consumption; Take-home risk assessment; Naloxone supply and training; Missed doses and engagement; Safeguarding children.
11. **Physical Health & Metabolic Monitoring.** Sections: Baseline checks; Antipsychotic monitoring; Smoking and lifestyle; Long-term conditions; Referrals; Follow-up.
12. **Observation & Engagement.** Sections: Level set and review; Handover; Recording quality; Engagement quality; Staffing allocation; Escalation.
13. **Risk & Safety Planning.** Sections: Initial assessment; Formulation; Safety plan; Review after change; Family and carers; Discharge risk.
14. **Bereavement & Family Support.** Sections: Pre-death support; Immediate after death; Follow-up contact; Memorial and letters; Staff support; Feedback.

# Care Certificate Assessor: Eight Questions an Inspector Could Ask

Usually the assessor is whoever manages the new starter, and nobody asks any more. A sharper habit is to test, standard by standard, whether that person can judge it. Below are eight questions for a care certificate assessor, with the evidence we would show in reply.

Our answers rest on one document: the Care Certificate standards assessor and employer guide. We call it the Assessor Guide. [Read the full Assessor Guide on the Skills for Care site](https://www.skillsforcare.org.uk/resources/documents/Developing-your-workforce/Care-Certificate/Care-Certificate-Standards/Care-Certificate-assessor-and-employer-guide-March-2025.pdf) to check any point.

Four bodies publish it together: the Department of Health and Social Care, NHS England, Skills for Care and Skills for Health. A shorter Skills for Care questions and answers document backs it up. We call that one the Q&A.

## Who is your assessor, and why that person?

The Assessor Guide gives the assessor one job: deciding whether a support worker has met the standards. To do it, the person must be competent in the standard they assess. For almost all assessors, that competence comes from a qualification related to the role.

One person need not cover all sixteen. That surprises many services. Basic life support, Standard 12, may call for a different assessor from the other fifteen.

We would pick a senior carer or a deputy over a registered manager who is already stretched. The trade off is rota time, so give the assessor protected hours. A manager who assesses in the gaps between calls will rush, and the evidence will show it.

## Does an assessor need an assessor qualification?

No. The Assessor Guide sets no such rule. The employer must simply be confident that the person is competent to assess. Without a relevant qualification, it suggests they work to National Occupational Standard CLDLD09, Assess learner achievement.

Some services look for care certificate assessor training. The Q&A points to free learning materials for assessors on the elearning for healthcare platform, so it is a choice and not a rule.

In our view the better test is simple, and shorter than any course. Could this person explain to an inspector why they judged a worker competent? Keep one line per assessor:

- Name and role.
- The standards they assess.
- Why the employer is confident they are competent.

## What did the assessor actually watch at work?

Look at the verbs. Where a standard says demonstrate, take steps to, use or show, the evidence must come from real work. The assessor stands in the room, or at the doorway, and watches it happen.

Take an example.

Outcome 7.2b covers privacy and dignity in personal care. The Assessor Guide lists examples such as knocking before entering and getting the curtains right. It adds that a worker need not show every example, nor show it a set number of times.

Each care certificate observation is a judgement. The assessor may be satisfied after one span of duty, or want more.

What goes on the record matters as much as the visit. We would note four things after every observation:

- The standard and outcome the visit evidenced.
- What the worker did, in plain words.
- The assessor's decision: met, or not yet met.
- The date, the assessor's name and the next step.

:::note
An invented example. Meera, a senior carer, shadows Callum through one morning shift in a residential home. She sees him knock, wait and close the curtain, and she records it against privacy and dignity. She also sees a missed hand wash before a meal, so she books a second visit for infection control.
:::

One visit can feed more than one standard. The Assessor Guide says evidence may count towards several, and it urges assessors to work this way. A good morning of personal care can show communication, privacy and hand hygiene together.

## Why was that skill shown in a classroom?

Sometimes that is allowed. Simulation is allowed only where a skill could not reasonably be assessed in real work, or is unlikely to occur during induction. Basic life support is the guide's own example.

Remote video and live recordings are a separate matter. The Assessor Guide rules them out where they would compromise the dignity and confidentiality of the people supported.

We would write one sentence on the file each time simulation was used, saying why real work was not possible. An inspector then sees a decision, not a shortcut.

## Where does the online course fit in care certificate assessment?

It covers knowledge. The Assessor Guide says eLearning is a way to acquire and show knowledge, not skill, and that eLearning alone cannot provide full achievement.

Where eLearning is used, it needs an assessment attached, such as questions and answers, so that the service can show what the worker actually learnt. Attendance alone proves nothing.

So the course sits in the file beside the observation. It never replaces it. Knowledge verbs such as describe, explain and identify can be answered in writing or aloud, says [the Q&A on assessing knowledge and understanding](https://www.skillsforcare.org.uk/resources/documents/Developing-your-workforce/Care-Certificate/Care-Certificate-Standards/Care-Certificate-standards-FAQs.pdf).

## How much evidence is enough?

Enough is what leaves the assessor confident. That judgement is theirs alone, says the Assessor Guide. A worker cannot be part skilled and still meet a standard, however much paper sits in the file. The care certificate competency assessment should be as rigorous as for any formal qualification.

Each piece of evidence faces five tests:

1. Valid: it relates to the standard being claimed.
2. Authentic: the worker produced it.
3. Current: it is recent enough to trust.
4. Reliable: it truly represents what the worker can do.
5. Sufficient: it meets the standard in full.

No limit applies to attempts. The employer decides what happens if a worker cannot meet a standard after proper support.

## When did this person start working out of sight?

Before the assessor had judged them competent. The Q&A expects regulated providers to assess a new support worker first. It adds that enough time must be planned for it.

Regulation 18 is the legal footing. Under the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, staff must get the support, training and supervision their work needs. See [the published text of Regulation 18](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2014/2936/regulation/18) for the exact words.

Direct supervision, with the worker in the supervisor's line of sight, should last until the worker is judged safe to be left alone with the people they support. Phasing helps. As each standard is met, supervision for that task can ease.

## Who can sign off the Care Certificate, and where is the record?

The employer. The Assessor Guide says the registered manager in adult social care signs the worker off as having met all the standards. They must be assured that the teaching and assessment were good enough.

That care certificate sign off cannot be outsourced. An employer may buy in training or assessment, says the Q&A, but it stays responsible for the award. Training firms may help with the learning, but they may not issue the certificate.

The award uses the approved national template. The employer keeps the record locally and makes it available to the worker. Where possible, it can also go into the Adult Social Care Workforce Data Set, known as ASC-WDS.

## Benefits of CareStream for your care certificate assessor

Our free Care Certificate course covers the knowledge side and leaves the judgement to your assessor.

- It takes {{minutes:care_certificate_course}} minutes and has {{count:course_questions}} questions.
- It includes a printable observed competency checklist, with lines for the assessor to tick and sign.
- The certificate is not issued until the manager records the observed sign off.
- The record keeps the name of the manager who signed and the date.
- A matrix shows who has attended and who is still missing, as in the figure below.

![CareStream face to face matrix listing staff by topic, with a Care Certificate refresher column and a green attended tick](https://www.carestreamai.com/matrix-f2f-matrix.jpg)

Figure: the matrix marks who has attended, so gaps show up before the next sign off.

CareStream does not award the Care Certificate. Your employer does, after your assessor has watched the work. The [free Care Certificate course](/staff-training/care-certificate) costs nothing on the free plan.

## What to do before the next starter arrives

Pick the assessor for each standard and write down why. Book the first observation into the rota in week one, before the starter has a full set of shifts to cover. Decide now who signs off. Then decide where the record will live.

Then keep the pieces together in one file: the knowledge results, each observation, and the sign off. Our [complete guide to Care Certificate training](/blog/the-complete-guide-to-care-certificate-training) covers the wider induction around it.

# Infection control audit: a walk round, a score and a plan

The reminder has popped up on the deputy's phone, and the laundry room is on the far side of the building. She has a tablet, forty minutes and a feeling that last quarter's infection control audit was mostly ticks. What should she actually look at, and what happens to a No once she has marked it?

This walk follows the free Infection Control audit in CareStream in the order you would do it on your feet. It ends with scoring and actions, because a list of findings that goes nowhere is the commonest weakness in an infection control audit.

## Start where the law starts

The main rule is Regulation 12, on safe care and treatment. It comes from the Regulated Activities Regulations made under the Health and Social Care Act 2008. Providers must assess the risk of infections and stop them spreading, as [the text of Regulation 12(2)(h)](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2014/2936/regulation/12) sets out.

A separate code of practice covers preventing and controlling infections. [The Health and Social Care Act 2008 code of practice on infections](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-health-and-social-care-act-2008-code-of-practice-on-the-prevention-and-control-of-infections-and-related-guidance) says the Care Quality Commission must take it into account. It is not mandatory.

Neither the regulation nor the code says "audit". Your audit, which many managers call an ipc audit, checks that the rules on paper are the rules on shift.

## Before you leave the office

Open the audit and read the set of sections once. The Infection Control audit has eight: General, Specimens, Waste, Laundry, Pest Control, Staff Health, Food Safety and Hygiene, and MRSA.

MRSA is a germ that resists several antibiotics. Not every section applies everywhere. A supported living service may have no specimens, so mark those questions not applicable rather than skipping them.

Take the tablet if you can. Answering on the spot beats typing from memory at your desk.

## Stop 1: the sink and the hands

General is the longest section, and its first real test is hand hygiene. Does the policy exist, yes. Do staff wash before, after and between care tasks? That one you cannot answer from a folder.

Stand in a corridor and watch. Watch the technique, not just the act. Check disposable towels, liquid soap and the notice by the sink.

If you want a stand alone hand hygiene audit tool, these questions are the heart of one. The same section asks about covering cuts, protective clothing, sharps, spillages of vomit or blood, and the plan for an outbreak.

## Stop 2: the sluice, the bins and the laundry room

Specimens, Waste and Laundry are short sections and quick to do together. Look at how things are labelled, sealed, bagged and kept apart. Is dirty laundry kept separate from clean? Is the bag big enough that nobody has to push it down?

Ask a care worker to show you, rather than tell you. A walk through the real route a bag takes from a bedroom to the machine will find more than any question will.

![Care worker in a mask beside a resident in a wheelchair while a colleague wipes a handrail, with a checklist clipboard in the corner](https://www.carestreamai.com/images/care-policies/infection-prevention-control/1.webp)

Figure: the habits to watch for on the walk, protective equipment worn and surfaces wiped.

## Stop 3: the kitchen door and the storeroom

Pest Control and Food Safety and Hygiene sit inside this audit, and that surprises some managers. Leftovers cleared, food covered, droppings absent, drains protected. These are infection risks as much as hygiene ones.

The food section also asks whether infection control training for cooks and food handlers is up to date. If it is not, the [free infection prevention and control course for staff](https://www.carestreamai.com/staff-training/infection-prevention-and-control) is one place to close that gap, free for every member of staff.

For the full food audit, we keep a separate Kitchen Audit. Run this one for the infection angle only.

## Stop 4: the people, then the records

Staff Health asks about screening, immunisation, early follow up of infectious illness and whether staff stay off work until safe to return. The answers sit in files, not on walls, so ask to see them.

MRSA asks whether a policy exists and whether the notes record people known to be infected. It also covers pressure sores, catheters, wounds and lines.

For guidance to put in front of staff, see the [UKHSA resource on infection prevention and control in adult social care](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/infection-prevention-and-control-in-adult-social-care-settings). It covers precautions, outbreaks and staff health.

## How to score it

Each check is answered Yes, No or Not applicable. A No has one more step: you say whether it was the correct answer or a gap, and the audit cannot be completed until you do.

Each section then shows a count and a percentage. The colour is green at 80 per cent or above, amber from 60 and red below.

No rule sets a pass mark, so these bands are ours. We suggest you read the colour second and the individual Nos first.

:::note
An invented example. Laundry scores 100 per cent and Waste scores 75 per cent, so Waste looks amber. But the one No is an overfilled sharps bin on a corridor, and that matters more than a clean laundry room.
:::

## From a No to a named action

Every check has a box for what was found and a box for actions to be taken. The audit also holds a deadline for actions and fields for strengths and improvements.

We suggest each action carries four things: what will change, who owns it, a due date and a way to prove it was done. Anything that puts a resident at risk is fixed that day, not at the next audit.

Close each action in writing. Providers must assess, monitor and improve the quality and safety of the service, and [Regulation 17 on good governance](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2014/2936/regulation/17) says so. An open action is an unanswered question.

## How often to repeat it

The template is set to quarterly, so that is a sensible starting rhythm for infection control audits for care homes. We know of no regulation that fixes the interval.

We would repeat a failed section sooner, and check again after any outbreak. Daily and weekly checks, such as a quick look at hand gel and PPE stocks, sit underneath the quarterly audit rather than replacing it.

Start the next audit by checking last time's actions. If the same No comes round twice, change the fix, not just the date.

## What an inspector can read in your record

The Care Quality Commission has a quality statement on infection control. It sits under the question on whether a service is safe. It begins "We assess and manage the risk of infection", as [the list of 34 quality statements](https://www.cqc.org.uk/publications/review-cqcs-single-assessment-framework-and-its-implementation/appendix-1-34-quality-statements) shows.

An audit record can feed that evidence for CQC infection control questions. It cannot promise a rating.

What helps is a dated trail: the audit, the scores, who owned each action and when it closed.

## Benefits of CareStream for your infection control audit

If you want an infection control audit template you can use today, CareStream has one.

- The Infection Control audit is one of the free audits on a free account, with no card needed.
- It works as an infection control audit tool on a tablet, with an actions box on each check.
- You can copy it and edit it, or build your own audit from scratch.
- Staff can take the infection prevention and control course free, so training and audit sit together.

See the [free audit library](https://www.carestreamai.com/care-audits) to open it.

## Run the walk on your own service

Pick one section, not all eight. Start with General, because hand hygiene shows more than any other check. Do it this week, with a colleague, and write down every No on an infection control audit checklist of your own, or on screen.

Then give each No an owner and a date. That is your infection prevention and control audit working as it should.

For the training side, our guide to [infection control training for care staff](https://www.carestreamai.com/blog/infection-control-training-for-care-staff-a-guide-for-managers) shows what staff need to know before you test them.

# Business continuity plan care home: the night the power failed

The lights drop out across the whole site, then come back dim, on the emergency circuit only. The heating has stopped and the lift will not move.

Someone on shift reaches for the business continuity plan care home owners are told to keep. Can they find it? Does it say what to do next?

:::note
An invented example. Larch House, its residents and its staff are made up, and nothing below happened to a real service.
:::

Larch House is a residential home. A fault on the supply cable has cut the power on a cold night, and the supplier cannot say when it will be back.

We follow the next few hours stage by stage. That is the test for any care home business continuity plan: does it still make sense when the person holding it is tired, in the dark and busy?

Along the way we tie each stage to the rules. The regulations never use the phrase business continuity plan, so a written plan is the way a service shows the rest.

## Stage one: someone decides this is an incident

The senior on shift walks the floors with a torch. Nobody is hurt. Residents are awake, a few are frightened, and two need the lift.

She does one thing before any other. She says aloud that this is an incident and that she is in charge until a manager says otherwise.

Plans fail here more than anywhere. If it is unclear who may declare an incident, people wait for permission. We suggest the plan names the role, not the person. It should list what counts: no power, no water, no heating, a flood.

## Stage two: the call list does its job

Next she calls. The plan gives her one page: the manager, the on call manager, the provider, the electricity network operator, the heating engineer and the nearest sister home.

That page earns its place or fails right now. A number that has been wrong since a manager left is a classic find in a desktop test.

We suggest holding the list on paper by the office phone, in a staff hub and on the on call mobile. Whichever one survives the failure gets used.

The legal root is Regulation 12, [the duty to provide safe care and treatment](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2014/2936/regulation/12). It asks providers to assess risks to people's health and safety and do all that is reasonably practicable to reduce them.

## Stage three: keeping people warm, fed and safe

The on call manager is on the phone within minutes. The senior now works down a short list.

- Warmth: blankets, extra layers, residents moved together into the smallest warm room.
- Light: torches and battery lamps in a known place, with a check that they work.
- Food and drink: cold meals and flasks, with a note of who needs thickened fluids or a special diet.
- Medicines: the round carries on by torchlight, and anything needing a fridge is checked and recorded.
- Equipment: who relies on a powered mattress, oxygen concentrator or hoist, and what the backup is.

Most of that is our suggestion about what a sensible plan holds. The law behind it is plain. [Regulation 15 on premises and equipment](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2014/2936/regulation/15) asks for premises that are clean, secure, suitable, properly used and properly maintained.

At Larch House the plan has a named person for each line, and a tick sheet. That is what makes the night calm.

![Care worker pushing a resident in a wheelchair towards an open door while a colleague points the way and holds a clipboard](https://www.carestreamai.com/images/care-policies/evacuation/1.webp)

Figure: if the building cannot be used, one person leads, one person moves people and someone keeps the list of who has gone where.

## Stage four: who has to be told, and when

By now the on call manager has spoken to the electricity company. Repair is estimated for the next morning. The question is who else hears about it.

The Care Quality Commission has its own rule. [Regulation 18 of the 2009 registration regulations](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2009/3112/regulation/18) says the registered person must notify the Commission without delay.

That covers a loss of utilities: gas, water, power or sewerage cut off for more than 24 hours in a row. It also covers any event likely to threaten safe care.

The Larch House cut may end before the 24 hours is up. The plan still says who decides whether it threatens safe care, and that the decision is written down with the reason.

Beyond the Commission, we suggest the plan lists the local authority commissioners, families and the provider's own senior team. It should say who rings whom, in what order and by what time.

## Stage five: stay, or move?

Hours pass and the repair slips. Now comes the hardest call in any plan: do people stay where they are, or move?

The decision belongs to a named manager, with the clinical lead if there is one. We suggest the plan says what tips the balance. Examples are a room that cannot be kept warm, or a person who depends on powered equipment.

[The Care Quality Commission guidance on Regulation 12](https://www.cqc.org.uk/guidance-regulation/providers/regulations-service-providers-and-managers/health-social-care-act/regulation-12) mentions plans with other providers for events such as fires and floods. In our view that means an agreement made in advance with a sister home. A first call on the night is too late.

If people do move, someone keeps a list of where each person went, what medicines and records travelled with them and who has been told.

## Stage six: the record, and what changes afterwards

Power returns in the early hours. The senior writes up the night while it is fresh: when it began, what was done, who was called and when, and how each resident fared.

Regulation 17 on good governance asks for systems that assess, monitor and mitigate risks to people, and for records that go with them. [The full text of Regulation 17 on good governance](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2014/2936/regulation/17) shows where this record fits.

The manager holds a short review within days. What worked, which number was wrong, and did the torches have batteries? Each answer changes the plan.

That review is the part inspectors can test. A plan updated after a real incident is a living document, not one that sat in a folder.

## What belongs in a business continuity plan template

The night at Larch House shows the parts in order. A business continuity plan template for care homes, or a plan for any business continuity plan social care service, should hold these. The same list suits a business continuity plan for care homes of any size:

- Who declares an incident, and who takes charge.
- The call list, kept current.
- Warmth, light, food, drink, medicines and equipment.
- Who is told, including the Care Quality Commission.
- The stay or move decision, and the arrangement with another home.
- The record, review and sign off.

A generic template cannot name your people, your supplier or your sister home. Those gaps are what a test finds first.

The business continuity policy sets out who is responsible and how often the arrangements are tested. The plan holds the detail used on the day. A care home emergency plan for fire has its own [fire safety policy](https://www.carestreamai.com/care-policies/fire-safety) beside it.

## Benefits of CareStream for your business continuity plan care home

If you hold a business continuity plan care home inspectors may ask about, CareStream can test the paperwork around it.

- Upload your document to the [free policy gap check](https://www.carestreamai.com/policy-gap-detection) and each regulation that applies comes back covered, partly covered or a gap.
- The check costs nothing and needs no card. It takes your first {{count:free_policy_checks}} policies.
- Policies are compared with each other, so a call list that disagrees with the fire procedure gets flagged.
- Where there is a gap, we write a business continuity policy for your service, check it by hand and deliver it within two working days.

## Run the power cut on paper

Take your own plan and play the night through. Who declares the incident? Does the call list work? Which numbers are out of date?

Run it with two seniors on different shifts and record what they could not find. Fix those gaps first. CareStream describes its business continuity feature as plans every staff member can open at any time.

If you hold no plan, or the test shows gaps, our [business continuity policy](https://www.carestreamai.com/care-policies/business-continuity) is written for your service. A plan on the shelf proves little until someone has tried it.
